docs.title: Recce
docs.text:
An open-source reconstruction engine that turns photographs into 3D models (camera poses, point clouds, meshes and gaussian splats) and says what it knows and what it does not: scale, frame, coverage and uncertainty.

The project is in Step 0: prototypes test the riskiest assumptions and mock-ups work out the product, side by side. The engine package recon holds its first code, a capture-set reader. Progress: Step 0 status and findings.

Section What it holds Concept The brief, the architecture sketch and the first use cases Reference Theory, tools, product analysis and datasets Licensing MIT, and the rules that keep it honest Working notes Research and reviews in progress

Source: chipi/recce.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
What is open, what is not, and how the project stays MIT while standing on tools that are not.

The project is open source from its first commit under the MIT licence (see LICENSE), like its sibling projects. MIT covers everything in this repository unless a file says otherwise: the engine, workers, faces (web UI, HTTP API, MCP server, CLI), the iPhone capture app, infrastructure as code, documentation and tests.

docs.title: Why MIT
docs.text:
• Consistent with the owner's other projects (Chemigram, Orrery), and the most widely understood permissive licence.
  • Compatible with the default stack. COLMAP and GLOMAP (BSD-3), gsplat and Brush (Apache-2.0), MapAnything's Apache checkpoint, SAM 2 (Apache-2.0), LightGlue (Apache-2.0 per its README), ALIKED (BSD-3), Open3D (MIT), Rerun (MIT or Apache-2.0), rawpy (MIT) over LibRaw (LGPL-2.1 or CDDL-1.0), mvs-texturing (BSD-3). MIT code may depend on all of these; their own licences keep applying to them. Sources: tools overview.
  • The alternative considered: Apache-2.0. It adds an explicit patent grant and a NOTICE convention. It would matter if contributors' patents were a real concern; for a project started by one person and its agents, MIT's simplicity wins. Apache-licensed dependencies are used under their own terms either way, and their NOTICE files ship with any bundled copy.

docs.title: The boundary rules
docs.text:
MIT stays honest only if nothing more restrictive is pulled into the MIT code. Three rules:

  1. Copyleft tools run as separate processes, never as imports. darktable (GPL, for the develop stage, possibly through Chemigram), OpenMVS and OpenSplat (AGPL), PyMeshLab (GPL-3.0): if used at all, they are optional plug-ins invoked as external programs, installed by the user, never vendored, never imported into the engine's Python process.
  2. Restricted model weights are never shipped. Non-commercial or custom-licensed weights — VGGT-1B, Pi3/Pi3X, MASt3R/DUSt3R, MapAnything's CC-BY-NC checkpoint, SAM 3, SuperPoint — are optional plug-ins the user downloads under the weights' own terms. Each plug-in states its licence in the stage registry, and every reconstruction's provenance records the licence of every implementation that touched it.
  3. No dataset lives in the repository. Public datasets are fetched by scripts, under their own licences, into a local cache outside git. Most of the useful ones are non-commercial (public datasets): fine for development and research results, not for redistribution. The benchmark code is MIT; the benchmark data is whatever its source allows.

docs.title: What is not in this repository
docs.text: Not here Where it lives Photos and captures (the owner's, friends', robots') Local storage; never committed Public datasets Local cache, fetched by script Restricted model weights Downloaded by the user per plug-in Secrets (tailnet keys, cloud credentials) Never committed; see the infrastructure docs when they exist

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• Refractive COLMAP (the main underwater candidate) is New BSD (verified 2026-11-24); it has no Python bindings, so it runs as a separately built program. It is permissive and may be vendored.
  • Test fixtures with real photos need their own licence per file (Chemigram uses CC BY-SA 4.0 for its raw fixtures); decided when the first fixture is added.

docs.title: Every capture is a mission
docs.text:
Someone, or something, goes into a place for a limited time and has to come back with a model that other people will act on. The limit differs: the air in a diver's tank, the twenty minutes in a drone's battery, the hour a robot can survive in a burned building, the afternoon a seller has the keys to a flat, the weekend a car is clean. What does not differ is the shape of the problem. The capture can only be judged after it is over, and by then the place is out of reach. The gap under the hull, the field the drone missed, the room the robot never entered, the staircase nobody photographed: all of them show up when it is too late to go back.

Recce makes the capture answer back while the mission is still running. After every leg of a mission (a dive, a battery, a pass through a building, a floor of a house) it shows, within the time before the next leg, what is already covered and what is missing, and where to go to close it. When the gaps are closed, it finishes the model with whatever power is within reach that night, and hands it over with a datasheet that says exactly how far it can be trusted. The point is not a model at the end. It is leaving the place knowing the model will hold.

docs.title: Five missions
docs.text:
Recce is built for very different people doing the same thing.

A diver documents a wreck for cultural heritage. The site is protected, deep and visited rarely; archaeologists will measure from the model for years. The mission is two or three dives a day with surface intervals between them. What cannot be redone: the season, the weather window, the boat.

A drone surveys terrain before something is built. Roads, houses, slopes and drainage are documented for a new project. The mission is a series of flights, one battery at a time. What cannot be redone cheaply: the crew on site, the permit, the light.

A small robot enters a place people should not. After a fire, or where a structure may come down, a robot or remote vehicle goes inside so that the people outside can see how it looks before anyone enters. The mission is one or a few passes on a weak radio link. What cannot be redone: the time, and possibly the robot.

An enthusiast wants a model of what they love. A car, a mountain bike, a camera, something built by hand. The mission is an afternoon with a phone or a camera. What cannot be redone: the car being clean, the light being right, the patience.

An estate agent sells a home. The flat inside and the building outside, measured, presented to buyers who will never visit in person. The mission is one visit with the keys. What cannot be redone: the empty flat, the agent's afternoon.

docs.title: What every mission shares
docs.text:
Underneath, every mission has the same five steps.

  1. Plan. What the model is for decides what it needs: an archaeologist needs scale and texture, a responder needs the layout and what was not seen, a buyer needs rooms that look right and measure right.
  2. Capture, in legs. Photographs, with whatever comes with them: the phone's position and depth, the drone's GPS, the robot's own poses.
  3. Preview, after every leg. In the time before the next leg, Recce adds the new photographs to the running model and shows a preview with its coverage: what is seen well, seen weakly, not seen at all, and where to stand to fix it.
  4. Full pass, when the gaps are closed. The heavy reconstruction (dense geometry, the mesh, the texture, the gaussian splat) runs once, overnight or while the person does something else.
  5. Hand-over. The model goes to whoever acts on it, with its datasheet: its true size or "size unknown", its frame, where it is solid, inferred or unseen, and how it was made.

The quick pass is what turns a capture into a conversation. The full pass is what makes the result worth keeping. The datasheet is what makes it usable by someone who was not there. Step 0 showed why the datasheet matters: on a scanned room, surfaces no photograph saw were 52.4 mm off the laser reference, surfaces seen by thirty-two or more were 14.7 mm off. A model that hides that difference cannot be measured from, handed to a robot or used to send people into a building.

docs.title: Two speeds
docs.text:
The preview: plan the next leg without waiting. As soon as a leg's photographs are on the laptop, Recce builds a preview from them: every camera in its place, the rough shape of the place, coverage laid over it, and the gaps with where to stand to close them. It is the quick pass: reduced photographs, each leg added to what came before instead of starting over, minutes rather than hours, on the laptop in the field and offline, or on the operator's station outside the burned building. The person walks around it, sees what the first dive or the first battery missed, and plans the second leg on it. Nobody waits for the full render to know what to do next. The preview does not need to be finished; it needs to be right about the gaps.

The preview builds in front of the person's eyes. There is no progress bar followed by a finished model. As the photographs come in (copied off the card, sent from the phone, streamed by the robot), each one is picked up and finds its place: the photo flies to where it was taken, the points it shares with the others light up, and the shape of the place grows out of them. The coverage fills in as it goes, and the gaps show up as the parts that stay dark. Everything stays live and interactive while it builds: the person turns the model, opens a photo, follows the threads to what it sees, and starts planning the next leg before the last photograph has landed. Watching a reconstruction happen is also how a person learns what makes one work.

The local client does the heavy lifting on the data. Everything that touches the camera's originals happens on the laptop: reading the RAW files, developing them into one consistent set (white balance, exposure, colour), dropping the blurred and the duplicates, placing every camera. That is what the Studio is for, beyond showing the preview: by the time anything leaves the laptop, it is only what the model needs, the working images at the resolution the full pass uses and the camera solution. A transfer that would take a hotel uplink most of a day takes minutes to an hour. The originals never leave the person's disk.

A darkroom in the Studio. Developing the photographs is its own craft, and Recce treats it as one: the RAW decoded, the lens corrected, white balance, exposure, tone and colour made to agree across the whole set, the way a photographer would in Lightroom, but for a reconstruction rather than a print. The person can open the develop panel, tune it and save what they like as a preset. Recce ships its own presets too, and those are not guesses: they come out of evaluation, the same develop settings tried on many scenes with known answers and kept where the models came out better (more photographs placed, colour that holds across seams, texture that stays sharp). A preset learned on a reef is different from one learned on a white-walled flat, and Recce says which it chose and why.

A recipe is how Recce remembers what works. A recipe is a named, versioned set of choices for a kind of mission: the develop preset, the lens and camera model, how photographs are matched and placed, how the full pass builds the surface and the splat, and the evidence that earned it, its scores on the scenes it was tested on. Recce proposes a recipe from what it sees (the camera, the photographs, the priors, the kind of mission) and says why; the person can keep it, change it or bring their own. The recipes and corrections learned from a person's own cameras and captures are theirs.

A workflow is how the person works. Not every mission needs every step. A GoPro's JPEGs can go straight in as they are; a D850's RAW files go through the darkroom first; a careful person stops to look at the develop panel before anything is matched, and someone in a hurry sends everything to the full pass the moment the gaps are closed. A workflow is the chain of steps a project runs, in the person's order: which steps are in, which are skipped, where Recce pauses for a look or an approval, where the full pass goes. The person builds it on a canvas, saves it, and keeps different workflows for different kinds of project; Recce proposes one for a new mission, with a recipe filling in each step's settings. A workflow can change in the middle of a mission: add the darkroom after the first leg shows the colour is off, and only the steps after the change run again. The workflow says what happens; the recipe says how well each step is tuned.

A project holds one place. A wreck, a building site, a flat, a car: each is a project, the boundary of one scene and everything done to it. A project holds two things. Its assets: the photographs of every leg, kept as ordinary files in the project's own folder on the person's disk, where any other tool can still open them. And its work: the workflow, the develop settings, the recipes, every run, every model and datasheet, and the history of the missions. Recce never changes an original; everything it does is stored as settings and results beside them, the way Lightroom keeps a catalog beside the photographs. Switching from one project to another is one click. Moving a project to another computer is copying its folder, or exporting it with or without the originals; on the other side Recce finds the photographs again by their content, so a renamed disk or a moved folder does not break anything.

Bringing photographs in. The person points Recce at a folder, or plugs in the camera, the drone's card or the phone, and Recce imports: the photographs go into the project's folder, one subfolder per leg, named by date and device, duplicates from a card imported twice left out. Robots and the capture app deliver the same way, over the network. Inside the project, a small library shows every photograph by leg, camera and time; any photograph opens in a viewer with its metadata (camera, lens, exposure, position, depth, where it sits in the model) and with what the darkroom has done to it, before and after.

The darkroom works on groups with the same light. A day's photographs do not share one light: the morning dive is blue and bright, the afternoon dive greener and darker; the drone's first battery flew in sun, the last in cloud. Recce groups the photographs of a project by leg, camera and measured light, and proposes those groups as the units of the darkroom. The person picks one photograph of a group, changes it, and sees the change live on that photograph and on the whole group as a contact sheet; applying it applies to the group, never touching the originals. Then Recce makes the groups agree with each other, because a reconstruction blends photographs from every leg into one surface, and two lights that disagree show up as seams on the model. The preview shows that too: a group out of line with the rest is visible on the model as a patch of the wrong colour, and fixing it in the darkroom fixes it there.

The full pass runs where the power is, and every case has some. Dense geometry, the mesh, the texture and the splat need a CUDA or HIP GPU and hours of it. Recce finds that power wherever the person has it:

  • in the laptop, when it has the GPU: the full pass runs there, nothing is sent;
  • next to the laptop: an external GPU or a GPU machine carried along, on the desk or in the van;
  • at home: the person's own machine with a GPU, reached over their private network;
  • rented by the hour, when they have none of these: a GPU from the person's own provider account, priced before it starts, approved by the person, gone when it ends. A night costs a few dollars.

Recce shows the time and the cost on each option before the person chooses. Nobody needs to own the big machine, and nobody who owns one is made to rent.

docs.title: Surfaces
docs.text:
The same product appears in a few places, built once.

Surface Who uses it Where What runs there Recce Studio (desktop, macOS and Windows, Linux too) The person running the mission Their laptop, in the field or at home The interface, the local engine, the quick pass; the full pass when the laptop has the GPU for it; sends the rest out Recce on the web The same person away from the laptop; anyone a model is shared with A browser, reaching the person's own home machine, or a shared link The same interface as the Studio; the viewer and the presentation for shared models Capture app (iPhone first) The person capturing with a phone On site Photographs with position and depth; live coverage while shooting; sends to the Studio Station for robots and vehicles A robot, a vehicle, its operator Beside the operator, or on the vehicle Receives capture sets, runs the quick pass, returns the brief for the next leg Workers Nobody directly Home machines, rented GPUs The full pass Agents A person's own agent Anywhere Everything above, through MCP

The Studio is the website, packaged. One web application (the interface, the 3D scenes, three.js and splats) is the Studio's interface and the browser's. On the desktop it is wrapped together with the local engine as a single installable application for macOS and Windows. The wrapper is Electron (owner, 2026-11-27): it ships its own Chromium, so the 3D scenes render the same on every system, and its size is small next to the engine it carries. What the browser shows and what the Studio shows is the same thing.

How a robot's mission runs with Recce. The robot's own software plans and drives; Recce sees and advises. With robotics-lab, whose Mission Control plans and executes the owner's robots, the shape proposed on both sides (2026-11-27, not yet decided by the operator) is:

  • A leg is a group of capture steps in the robot's mission plan: a sequence of capture_view goals, each a place to stand and a burst to shoot.
  • During the leg, a reduced stream goes out. The robot's recording keeps every frame and sends a reduced copy with poses over its link to a Recce station. The robot does the cheap selection (a rate, or a new frame when the pose has changed enough), within the link's budget; Recce does the selection that needs the model (what adds coverage). The full set follows when the robot is back or the link is good.
  • The station sits beside Mission Control on the operator's machine; later, as an option, on the robot's own computer for when the link drops.
  • After the leg, the gaps come back as data (gaps.json). The planner treats "a capture with open gaps" as a reason to replan, at the leg boundary; it turns the gaps into the next leg's capture steps, the operator reviews, and Mission Control executes. In manual mode the operator sees the gaps and adds the leg by hand. Recce never steers the robot.
  • In a hazard, unseen is not the same as unsafe. For the robot in a burned building, the gaps have to say whether a part is merely unseen or lies behind something the model marks as dangerous, so the planner does not send the robot there, and each leg has a time budget the preview must meet. This is a safety design the operator decides with robotics-lab, not only an interface.

A vehicle with its own computer can carry the station on board and send only the coverage and the gaps.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text:
For every mission:

  • No one goes back to a site because of a gap Recce could have shown before they left.
  • The quick pass after each leg arrives before the next leg starts.
  • The full pass runs on power the person did not have to buy, at a cost they saw before they approved it.
  • Every model that leaves Recce carries its datasheet, and what the datasheet says holds against a reference.
  • The photographs and the models never leave the person's control unless they send them.

For each mission:

  • The diver closes the morning's gaps in the afternoon dive and leaves the site with a model the archaeologists measure from without asking how it was made.
  • The drone crew packs up after the last battery knowing the area is covered, and the next morning's terrain meets the control points.
  • The responders see the inside of the building within the hour, with the unseen parts marked as unseen, before anyone walks in.
  • The enthusiast gets a model they are proud to show, from a phone and an evening of rented power, and reshoots less each time because Recce explained what went wrong.
  • The agent leaves the flat with every room covered and sends buyers a walk-through the same day, with sizes that hold.

docs.title: What makes Recce
docs.text:
Answers while the mission runs. The preview grows live from the first photograph of every leg; no tool offers that today, the others answer after the mission is over.

Power without owning it. The heavy work goes where the hardware is, at home or rented for a night, decided and paid for by the person.

Models that state their limits. The datasheet travels with every model: true size or not, solid or inferred or unseen.

One mission shape for people, robots and agents. The same brief goes to a person as cards on a screen, to a robot as data, to an agent through MCP.

Places with a history. A wreck visited each season, a site before and after construction, a building before and after the fire, a home sold twice: each becomes a place Recce remembers. The next mission starts from the last one's gaps.

It explains and it teaches. Every stage is something to look at and understand. Small labs inside the product show the physics behind a weak capture. A person's own AI, when they connect one, coaches on top: why the capture came out the way it did and what to do about it, its numbers checked against Recce's. Without AI, Recce is complete.

It is the person's. Open source, running on their machines, with no Recce cloud to send anything to.

docs.title: Why now
docs.text: Global camera solving made registration three to four times faster, which is what makes a quick pass between legs thinkable. Gaussian splats made reconstructions something people want to look at. Phones record their own position and depth with every photograph, and robots and drones carry the same. A CUDA GPU rents for about a third of a dollar an hour. Agents can drive tools, and local models run beside them. The established tools were built for one large machine and a finished set of photographs; none of them is built for a mission that is still running.

docs.title: Where it starts
docs.text:
At home, with the phone and the Studio. The capture app and an object on a table, then a whole room. It is the enthusiast's and the estate agent's mission at its smallest, and the room is the robots' world.

The quick pass and the full pass, split, from the start. In parallel: the quick pass on the laptop and the full pass on a rented GPU and home machines, measured at every hand-off (what is sent, how long it takes, what it costs, how long each pass runs). Borrowed power and the quick pass are what every mission depends on, so they are built first.

The drone, the dive and the robot in a hazard follow on the same shape; Step 0 already measured what each of them needs (RTK and control points, the refractive camera model and colour in water, a robot's capture set and frame).

docs.title: The bets
docs.text:
1. The quick pass fits between legs. Coverage and the next shots for a leg's photographs arrive within a surface interval, a battery swap, or live for a robot.
  2. The quick pass is right about the gaps. What it calls covered is covered in the full pass.
  3. What travels is small enough. The working set crosses a field connection in minutes to an hour without costing the model its quality.
  4. A night of borrowed power is enough, at a price one person accepts.
  5. The datasheet is honest against references, on real missions.

docs.title: What Recce refuses to be
docs.text: Not a cloud service: there is no Recce server to send photographs to. Not a survey instrument: models state their limits instead of claiming a grade. Not the controller of robots or drones: they capture with their own software, and Recce tells them what is missing. Not dependent on AI.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• The preview. At which reduced resolution, how it adds a leg without starting over, how fast it runs on a laptop without a GPU, and how close it looks to the final model.
  • The robot link. The transport for the reduced stream over a weak link and its back-pressure; the hazard rules for unseen against unsafe (with robotics-lab and the operator).
  • What the full pass needs sent, and when the originals have to travel (full-detail texture, colour corrected by range underwater).
  • Renting. Which providers first, and how data reaches them.
  • The develop module. Which libraries for lens correction and colour, and how presets are evaluated across scenes; how light groups are found and matched across legs; its own prototypes.
  • The project format. What the project file holds, how an export carries the originals or only the working set, and how a project on two computers stays in step.
  • A Mac running the full pass itself, or always sending it out.

docs.title: Architecture sketch — the logical shape
docs.text:
Working sketch for discussion. Input to the Step 0 prototypes and to RC-04 Technical Architecture. Written before any prototype exists, so every component here is a hypothesis the prototypes test, and every library choice is a candidate, not a decision.

Version: 0.1 · Draft · 2026-11-23 Inputs: brief · tools overview · primer · hardware · robotics-lab contract

docs.title: 1. The shape in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart TB

    H[Person: browser on laptop or phone]

    A[Agents: MCP clients]

  end

  subgraph Faces["Faces (thin, no logic of their own)"]

  end

  subgraph Engine["Engine (on the X3; on the laptop when alone)"]
    SVC[Engine service<br/>one API all faces call]
    MODEL[(Reconstruction model<br/>the scientific core)]
    GRAPH[Pipeline graph<br/>stages, params, cache]
    QUAL[Quality and comparison]
    COORD[Coordinator<br/>partition, place, retry]
    STORE[(Artifact store<br/>content-addressed)]
  end

  subgraph Workers["Workers (one per machine, join and leave)"]
    W1[M4 Pro<br/>Metal / CPU]
    W2[GB10<br/>CUDA]
    W3[X3<br/>HIP / Vulkan / CPU]
    W5[Rented cloud GPUs<br/>CUDA, ephemeral]
  end

  H --> UI
  P --> API
  R --> CLI
  A --> MCP
  S --> API
  UI --> SVC
  API --> SVC
  MCP --> SVC
  CLI --> SVC
  SVC --> MODEL
  SVC --> GRAPH
  SVC --> QUAL
  GRAPH --> COORD
  COORD <--> W1 & W2 & W3 & W5
  W1 & W2 & W3 & W5 <--> STORE
  MODEL <--> STORE

Three rings. Faces translate a request into a call on the engine service and render the answer; they hold no logic. The engine owns the reconstruction model, decides what work to do and where, and judges the result. Workers do the computation and know nothing about projects, people or agents — they receive a task, fetch its inputs by hash, run one stage, and return outputs by hash.

docs.title: 2. The reconstruction model — the core everything is built around
docs.text:
The engine's centre is one structured model of a reconstruction. Every face shows it, every stage reads and writes it, every comparison is between two of them.

erDiagram
  PROJECT ||--o{ CAPTURE : has
  CAPTURE ||--o{ IMAGE : contains
  SENSOR ||--o{ IMAGE : took
  SENSOR ||--|| CALIBRATION : "has (estimated or given)"
  IMAGE ||--o| POSE_PRIOR : "may carry (GPS, ARKit, robot)"
  PROJECT ||--o{ RECONSTRUCTION : "has (variants)"
  RECONSTRUCTION ||--o{ POSE : "estimates per image"
  RECONSTRUCTION ||--o{ TRACK : "triangulates"
  RECONSTRUCTION ||--o{ PRODUCT : "derives"
  RECONSTRUCTION ||--|| FRAME : "is expressed in"
  PRODUCT }o--|| FRAME : "is expressed in"
  RECONSTRUCTION ||--o{ PROVENANCE : "records every step"
  PRODUCT ||--o{ PROVENANCE : "records"
Entity What it holds Why it is first-class Project The boundary of one scene: a folder on disk holding the originals (one subfolder per capture), and a project file with the workflow, develop settings, recipes, reconstructions and history (owner, 2026-11-27) Switching, moving and exporting work by project; originals are referenced by content hash, so a moved folder relinks Capture A set of images from one session and device (a leg), with how they were taken Underwater, drone, turntable and robot captures behave differently; the engine needs to know which it has Develop group Images of one project that share their light (by capture, camera and measured light), the unit a darkroom edit applies to, plus the matching that makes groups agree Light changes between legs; one set-wide setting cannot hold a morning and an afternoon dive Image File hash, decoded form, EXIF/XMP, mask, develop settings Content-addressed so a re-run never re-decodes; develop settings are part of provenance Sensor + Calibration Camera model (pinhole, Brown, fisheye, later refractive), intrinsics, their uncertainty, source (EXIF guess, given, estimated) One body and lens shared across images; robots and ARKit give calibrations, the engine estimates the rest Pose prior Pose from GPS, ARKit, gimbal or a robot, with frame, source (truth/belief/device) and uncertainty Priors are inputs the engine uses and reports on, never silently trusted or ignored Reconstruction Estimated poses, tracks, sparse points, the parameters and stage versions that produced them A project holds several — classical vs learned, with vs without priors — and compares them Frame Named frame, axes, units, and scale state: metric, metric-from-priors, scaled-by-markers or arbitrary The "main trap" robotics-lab named: a model never leaves without saying what its scale means Product Dense cloud, mesh, texture, splat, asset export, each with its frame Products are derived and replaceable; the poses are the asset Provenance Inputs (hashes), stage, implementation, version, parameters, machine, time, licence of the implementation Same input and parameters give the same output; licence travels with the result Quality Per image, per track, per region: registered or not, reprojection error, track length, coverage, uncertainty What the UI draws and an agent reads to say "capture more here"

On disk the model is language-neutral: a documented schema (JSON for structure, Arrow/Parquet for large tables such as tracks and points), with COLMAP's format as an import/export, never as the internal truth. This is what keeps a future Rust coordinator or worker possible.

docs.title: 3. The pipeline — stages as a graph
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  I[Ingest] --> D[Develop]
  I --> FS[Frame select<br/>video only]
  FS --> D
  D --> M[Mask]
  D --> F[Features]
  M --> F
  F --> PR[Pair select]
  PR --> MA[Match]
  MA --> SFM[Poses<br/>SfM]
  L[Learned first pass] -.priors and scale.-> SFM
  D --> L
  SFM --> BA[Bundle adjust<br/>+ scale + frame]
  BA --> DN[Dense depth]
  DN --> MS[Mesh]
  MS --> TX[Texture]
  BA --> SP[Splat]
  TX --> EX[Export / assets]
  SP --> EX
  BA --> Q[Quality]
  DN --> Q
  SP --> Q
  TX --> CC[Colour correct<br/>underwater, after geometry]
  CC --> EX

Each stage is a node with typed inputs, typed outputs and parameters. A node's output is cached under the hash of its inputs, parameters and implementation version, so changing one parameter re-runs only what depends on it (Meshroom's node graph works this way). Each stage has one or more implementations, each tagged with its licence and the backends it runs on.

Stage Job Default candidates (permissive) Optional plug-ins Runs best on Ingest Read files, metadata and priors; validate capture sets rawpy/LibRaw (NEF, ARW, DNG), pillow-heif (HEIC), PyAV/ffmpeg (video), exiftool (EXIF/XMP), gpmf-parser (GoPro), robot manifest reader — Any, CPU Develop Decode RAW to linear, lens correction, set-wide white balance, exposure, tone and colour matching; presets (its own module, owner, 2026-11-27) Own pipeline over third-party libraries: rawpy + numpy today (RC-P5); lens correction and colour libraries to evaluate darktable CLI (GPL; external tool) Any; CPU or GPU array ops Frame select Pick sharp, well-spaced frames from video Sharpness and overlap scoring, own code — Any Mask Separate object from background SAM 2 (Apache-2.0) SAM 3 (custom licence, CUDA 12.6+), rembg GPU: GB10, M4 (MPS), X3 Features Keypoints and descriptors per image COLMAP SIFT; ALIKED SuperPoint (restrictive weights) Fan-out across all machines Pair select Choose which image pairs to match Exhaustive, sequential, retrieval, spatial from priors — Coordinator Match Match descriptors, verify geometry COLMAP matcher; LightGlue (Apache-2.0 weights per its README) with ALIKED RoMa dense matching Fan-out across all machines Learned first pass Fast poses, depth and metric scale as priors MapAnything Apache checkpoint VGGT, Pi3X, MASt3R (non-commercial) GB10 (CUDA, memory) Poses (SfM) Register images, triangulate tracks GLOMAP (global), COLMAP (incremental) via pycolmap Refractive COLMAP (underwater; New BSD, separate C++ build, no pycolmap) X3 (strong CPU, big memory) Bundle adjust + frame Refine, apply priors, fix scale and frame, Sim(3) to the given frame COLMAP/Ceres via pycolmap; AprilTag markers; own Sim(3) alignment — X3 Dense depth Depth map per view, fused cloud COLMAP PatchMatch stereo (CUDA, or a HIP build) OpenMVS (AGPL) GB10 (CUDA), X3 (HIP build, unproven); no COLMAP dense path on the Macs Mesh Surface from dense cloud Poisson (Open3D), TSDF fusion for RGB-D — X3, GB10 Texture UV unwrap, blend, bake Candidates to evaluate: mvs-texturing (BSD-3), xatlas OpenMVS texturing (AGPL) X3 Splat Gaussian splat from the same poses gsplat (CUDA); Brush (wgpu: Metal, Vulkan) WaterSplatting (underwater) GB10 (gsplat), M4 and X3 (Brush) Colour correct Underwater colour using range from the model Own Sea-thru-style implementation — Any Export / assets Decimate, LODs, glTF/GLB, USDZ, PLY, splat formats trimesh, Open3D, a glTF writer, splat-transform (SPZ/SOG) — Any Quality Metrics, coverage, comparisons Own code over the model — Coordinator

The registration core. Features → pair selection → matching → view graph → poses → bundle adjustment is the part that turns an unordered pile of photos into positioned cameras with no help. It is the heart of the engine: every product downstream depends on it, it holds most of the "smart", and it is where most compute time on large sets goes (features and matching), so it is also where distribution pays most. Its outputs are not only poses but a verdict per image (registered, rejected and why) and the shape of the view graph (connected components, weak links), which the quality module and capture advice read.

Licences come from the tools overview; anything still unverified there is confirmed before it becomes a default.

The packaging reality (tools overview, 2026-11-23). The current pycolmap (4.2.1) ships wheels only for Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 and Windows — none for the GB10 (Linux aarch64); its CUDA wheels are Linux x86_64 only. So the GB10 needs source builds or containers for the core stack. (PyTorch, Open3D, rawpy and rerun-sdk ship no macOS x86_64 wheels either, one reason the Intel iMac Pro left the design on 2026-11-24.) Whether PyTorch's ROCm wheels cover the X3's GPU (gfx1151) is unknown. RC-P1 and RC-P2 turn these expectations into facts.

docs.title: Configurability — strategies, recipes, evidence
docs.text:
Different captures want different strategies: global SfM for a thousand-image reef, incremental for a small sequential set, a learned first pass for low-texture interiors, a refractive camera model underwater. The engine is modular on purpose, in five layers:

  1. Stage contracts. Each stage has a fixed contract: typed inputs, typed outputs, the quality numbers it must report. "Poses" takes a verified view graph and calibrations and returns poses, tracks and per-image verdicts — whoever computes them.
  2. Implementations (strategies). Each contract has one or more implementations in a registry — poses/glomap, poses/colmap-incremental, poses/learned-then-ba — each tagged with its licence, backends, version and parameters with defaults. Adding a strategy never changes the engine; it registers against a contract.
  3. Recipes. A recipe is a named, versioned choice of implementation and parameters per stage, plus fallback rules. Recipes match capture types: object-turntable, object-walkaround, interior, aerial, underwater, robot-capture. A recipe is data, saved with every reconstruction it produced.
  4. Selection. The engine proposes a recipe from evidence — EXIF and XMP (a drone's GPS and gimbal, a GoPro's fisheye), image count, whether frames are sequential, which priors are present, the capture type the owner tagged — and says why. The owner or an agent accepts, switches, or overrides single parameters.
  5. Fallbacks. A recipe declares what to do when a stage underperforms: if global SfM registers too few images, re-run incremental on the leftovers; if texture is low, add the learned first pass. Every fallback taken is recorded and shown.
recipe: underwater-survey
version: 1
stages:
  develop:   { impl: develop/minimal, params: { wb: set-wide } }
  pairs:     { impl: pairs/retrieval, params: { k: 40 } }
  poses:     { impl: poses/glomap }
  fallback:  { when: "registered < 0.9", then: { poses: poses/colmap-incremental, scope: unregistered } }
  colour:    { impl: colour/range-aware }

Workflows (owner, 2026-11-27). Above the recipe sits the person's workflow: which of these stages a project runs and in what order, which are skipped (a GoPro's JPEGs need no develop), where the run pauses for review or approval (the develop panel, a rented GPU), and where each pass runs. A workflow is saved, reused per kind of project and edited during a mission; since every stage's output is content-addressed, an edit re-runs only the stages downstream of it. The recipe fills each stage of a workflow with its implementation and parameters. RC-M4's recipe graph is the first picture of this canvas.

Three levels of control. Automatic (the engine picks), recipe (the owner picks a named strategy), expert (any parameter). The UI leads with the first two and keeps the third one disclosure away; the API and MCP expose all three.

Configurability is made scientific by comparison. Because stage outputs are cached by hash, a variant that changes only the pose strategy re-runs only from that stage. Two strategies on one capture become two reconstructions side by side with the same metrics — the comparative form of parallelism. Over time the owner's own captures, with measured reference dimensions, become a benchmark set: every recipe change runs against it, and "GLOMAP is better for reefs" stops being an opinion and becomes a table.

Restraint. An implementation earns its place in the registry with benchmark evidence, and defaults stay opinionated. The goal is the right strategy chosen for you and shown to you, not a wall of options.

docs.title: 4. Distribution — how work spreads over the machines
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Laptop (field)
  participant C as Coordinator (X3)
  participant G as GB10 worker
  participant M as M4 worker
  participant X as X3 worker
  L->>C: upload images (resumable, streamed)
  C->>C: hash, store, plan graph
  par per-image fan-out
    C->>M: extract features [img 1..n]
    C->>G: extract features [img n+1..2n]
    C->>X: extract features [img 2n+1..]
  end
  par per-pair fan-out
    C->>G: match pairs [block A]
    C->>X: match pairs [block B]
  end
  C->>X: poses (SfM) + bundle adjust
  C->>G: dense depth / splat (CUDA)
  C-->>L: progress, quality, previews (event stream)

Units of work. A task is one stage applied to one piece: a block of images, a block of pairs, a spatial cluster, a set of views for dense depth. The coordinator picks the piece size per stage so a task takes seconds to minutes — big enough that transfer is cheap relative to compute, small enough that a lost worker costs little.

Five forms of parallelism, each a way of cutting the graph:

Form Cut Example Fan-out By item Features per image, matches per pair, depth per view Spatial partition By region A reef split into overlapping clusters, each posed on a different machine, merged by shared images Streaming By time Features start while photos still upload; a coarse preview builds before the last image arrives Comparative By variant Classical and learned pipelines run at once on different machines; their difference is a quality signal Placement By capability Dense depth to CUDA, Brush splats to Metal or Vulkan, SfM to the biggest CPU and memory

Workers advertise, the coordinator places. A worker reports its backends (CUDA, MPS, HIP, Vulkan, CPU), memory, which stage implementations it has installed, and whether it is available — on a machine whose GPU is shared with other workloads, that includes whether the GPU is free now. The coordinator never sends work a machine cannot run.

Data moves by hash, not by shared path. Metashape's workers need shared storage mounted at the same path on every machine. Here a worker fetches inputs from the artifact store by content hash and caches them; a second task on the same images costs no transfer. This is what lets a laptop on a weak connection, a box on the tailnet and a rented GPU join one pool.

Rented workers burst the pool. When a job is bigger than the homelab — a reef survey, a building — the owner rents GPUs from a cloud provider and they join the pool for the job's duration, then go away. This shapes the design in six ways:

  • A worker is a deployable artifact. Container images per backend (CUDA x86_64, CUDA arm64, ROCm, CPU) for Linux machines, rented or owned; a native install for the Macs. The same image runs on the GB10 and on a rented box.
  • Infrastructure as code. A worker pool on a provider is declared in Terraform or OpenTofu: machine type, count, region, image, lifetime. apply adds workers, destroy removes them. No hand-built cloud machines.
  • Joining is automatic. A rented worker boots, joins the tailnet as an ephemeral node with a pre-issued, expiring key, registers with the coordinator, and advertises its capabilities like any other worker.
  • Ephemeral and interruptible. Spot or preemptible machines can vanish; small, idempotent, content-addressed tasks (already the design) make a lost worker cost one task's retry.
  • Cost and data gravity are placement inputs. A rented worker has a price per hour, and the owner's home upload bandwidth is the bottleneck for sending it photos. The coordinator weighs both: a rented GPU earns its place on compute-heavy stages over data it already holds, not on per-image work over a slow uplink.
  • Leaving home is a project setting. Interior, robot and private captures may forbid rented workers; the coordinator never places their data outside the owner's machines. Renting costs money, so starting a pool always needs a human's go — an agent can propose one, not start it.

Alone is a pool of one. The laptop runs the coordinator and a worker in one process tree when offline; nothing in the design requires a second machine. What a pool of one can do is bounded by its hardware: on the M4 Pro today that is ingest, develop, registration and a Brush splat, but not COLMAP dense depth (CUDA or HIP only) or gsplat (CUDA) — see the tools overview platform matrix. A portable dense path is an open question (§10).
