docs.text:
Face Who What it does Candidate stack Web UI The person Upload, watch progress, inspect cameras and points, compare variants, view mesh and splat, measure, export SvelteKit (as in Orrery), three.js, a splat renderer (Spark or similar), served by the engine HTTP API Programs, the iPhone app Projects, uploads, runs, results, quality; an event stream for progress Python ASGI service (FastAPI or Litestar), OpenAPI schema, server-sent events MCP server Agents Start and steer runs, read quality, compare, recommend captures — over the same engine service Official MCP Python SDK CLI recon Robots, scripts The file contract: a capture set in, a model plus provenance.json out Python entry point; no server required iPhone capture app (prototype RC-P11) The person in the field Capture with ARKit poses, intrinsics and LiDAR depth; write the shared capture-set format (the robots' format); send straight to the API Swift, ARKit

The rule from robotics-lab's Observatory carries over: anything a page shows is something a command or tool answers, and the reverse. The coordinate frame and scale state appear on every view.

docs.title: 6. Use cases through the architecture
docs.text: Use case Enters by Stages that matter most Where it runs Leaves as Household object, iPhone Web upload (HEIC/ProRAW) Develop, mask, SfM, dense, mesh, texture, splat Laptop alone, or X3 + GB10 GLB mesh + splat, metric if a marker or ARKit priors Lego, DSLR turntable Web upload (NEF/ARW) Develop (RAW), mask (turntable background), fine-detail dense X3 + GB10 High-detail textured mesh House interior Capture-app export with ARKit poses and LiDAR Priors into SfM, TSDF fusion from depth, low-texture handling X3 + GB10 Metric mesh in a room frame; splat for viewing Robot capture set CLI recon with the manifest Priors (truth/belief), Sim(3) to world/map, provenance X3 (+ GB10) mesh.ply/cloud.ply, provenance.json, stated scale Building, drone Web upload (JPEG/DNG with GPS and gimbal XMP) Spatial pair selection from GPS, partition, georeference All machines Georeferenced mesh, splat Underwater reef or wreck Web upload (GoPro video, DSLR RAW) Frame select, develop, refraction-aware model (later), partition, colour correct after geometry All machines Colour-corrected mesh and splat, scaled by bars or lasers Game-engine asset Any of the above Mesh cleanup, decimation, LODs, PBR texture, de-lighting X3 GLB for Godot, Blender, Unity, Unreal; USDZ Agent steering MCP Quality, comparison, capture advice Coordinator Recommendations, re-runs with new parameters Comparative run Any face Two reconstructions from one capture Different machines at once A difference report

docs.title: 7. Why these choices
docs.text: Choice Because Instead of One engine service, thin faces Four faces stay consistent; nothing a person can do is out of reach for an agent Separate backends per face Reconstruction model as the core, COLMAP as interchange Carries frames, scale state, uncertainty and provenance that COLMAP's format does not COLMAP's database as internal truth Content-addressed artifacts Determinism, caching, and workers without shared mounts A shared network path (Metashape's approach) Pipeline graph with cached nodes Change one parameter, re-run only what depends on it; comparisons are cheap Monolithic batch runs Stage implementations tagged by licence and backend Permissive default stack; non-commercial and AGPL tools as labelled plug-ins; placement by capability Picking one tool per stage forever Python first, language-neutral schema Next to pycolmap, PyTorch, gsplat, rawpy; Rust stays possible where measured Rust or C++ from day one Classical SfM verifies the learned pass Learned models are fast and give scale but run at low resolution; bundle adjustment is the accuracy check Trusting either alone Colour correction after geometry Sea-thru needs range per pixel, and the model supplies it Correcting before matching Stage contracts with registered strategies, bundled into recipes One capture type's best strategy is another's worst; strategies are swapped and compared without touching the engine One fixed pipeline, or raw options everywhere A benchmark set of the owner's captures with measured dimensions Strategy defaults rest on measured results, not opinion Defaults chosen by reputation Same poses for mesh and splat One scene, two products that agree; a splat for viewing, a mesh for measuring and assets Separate pipelines per product

docs.title: 8. Cross-cutting
docs.text:
• Determinism and provenance. Every product records input hashes, implementation, version, parameters, machine and time; randomness is seeded.
  • Frames and scale never hidden. Every product carries its frame and scale state.
  • Observability, without the content. Engine and workers send logs, metrics and traces to an existing observability stack; a run's trace shows which machine did what and how long transfers took. Telemetry carries ids, hashes, stage names, sizes, timings and error classes — never file names, paths, EXIF, GPS, image content or capture notes. A file name from a home scan ("kids bedroom.heic") is content. Telemetry never leaves the owner's machines.
  • Security. Workers and faces are reachable on the tailnet only; no public exposure in the concept phase.

docs.title: Storage and retention — conservative by default
docs.text:
Storage is budgeted by what can be recomputed. Three classes:

Class What Rule Keep Original captures; capture-set manifests; final products (poses, sparse model, mesh, texture, splat, exports); provenance and quality records Kept on the coordinator until the owner deletes the project. Never evicted automatically. Cache Decoded and developed images, features, matches, depth maps, intermediate clouds Content-addressed and recomputable. Evicted least-recently-used under a per-machine cap; a project's cache can be dropped after its products are final. Scratch A task's working files on a worker Deleted when the task finishes. Rented workers hold only scratch and cache and are destroyed with their disks.

Defaults are small and raised deliberately: a cache cap per machine (starting point: 10% of the volume's free space, at most 200 GB), a warning when a project's keep-class data passes a set size, and a dry-run report before any eviction. More space comes from an external disk attached to a machine and registered as a storage volume — the store does not care which disk holds an object, only its hash.

Deletion reaches every copy. The coordinator records which workers hold which hashes. Deleting a project removes its keep-class objects, purges the matching cache entries on every worker that reports holding them, and lists any worker that was offline so the purge completes when it returns. Rented workers are destroyed, not purged. Deletion produces a receipt: what was removed, where, and what is pending. Interior and robot captures hold faces, screens and documents, so their projects default to "stays home" (§4) and deletion is the expected end of their life, not an exception.

docs.title: 9. Leanings agreed with the owner (2026-11-23)
docs.text:
Recommendations for the prototypes to confirm, not locked decisions.

  • Coordinator–worker plumbing: our own small pull-based protocol. Workers register capabilities and pull leased tasks over HTTP; heartbeats and retries; data by hash. Placement (capabilities, GPU availability, cost, data gravity, may-leave-home) is the differentiator and no framework's scheduler knows those concepts. RC-P7 builds the minimum; if it outgrows a small module, Ray is reconsidered on that evidence.
  • One three.js scene for the product UI. Cameras, points (LOD streaming for large clouds), meshes and splats (a three.js splat renderer; Spark the candidate) in one scene, so overlays, picking and measurement work once. A Rerun export as the engineering inspection view and the bridge to robotics-lab. RC-P6 proves splat/mesh mixing and iPhone performance.
  • Capture advice, layered. Regions in the model's frame with measured deficits are the stored fact; image ids are their evidence; viewpoints are derived on request per actor (person, robot, drone) and only when the scale is metric. MVP: regions + image evidence. v1: viewpoints, including capture requests to robotics-lab in its world frame.
  • Splats in the MVP, bounded. One splat per reconstruction from the same poses, default parameters, GLB (KHR_gaussian_splatting) and PLY, in the same viewer, with held-out-view PSNR/SSIM as a quality metric. Brush on the laptop alone. Out of MVP: splat editing, mesh-from-splat, underwater splats, splat LOD/tiles.

docs.title: 10. Open questions (feed RC-04 and the prototypes)
docs.text:
1. Engine language beyond the first version: Python throughout, or Rust for the coordinator and worker agent? Closes on RC-P1, RC-P2 and RC-P7 evidence.
  2. Artifact store: plain content-addressed files on the X3, an object store, or both? The retention classes and cache rules are settled (§8, Storage and retention); the backing store and the exact cache caps are open.
  3. Metadata store: SQLite per project, or one Postgres for the engine?
  4. Coordinator–worker protocol — leaning: own pull-based protocol (section 9). Open: lease length, transport details, and the evidence threshold for revisiting Ray.
  5. Partitioning large registrations: how the view graph is cut into clusters, solved on different machines and merged through shared images, and whether GLOMAP's global approach changes the answer.
  6. Which stages actually run on Metal and ROCm today, and which fall back to CPU (RC-P1, RC-P2).
  7. Texturing: which permissive implementation is good enough, or whether texturing is built.
  8. Refraction: adopt Refractive COLMAP (New BSD; a separate C++ build without Python bindings, not merged upstream) or implement a refractive camera model.
  9. The develop step: own pipeline or darktable (RC-P5 chose the minimal rawpy route). Now its own module (owner, 2026-11-27), usable and testable alone: which libraries for lens correction (lens profiles from a database, or the calibration the reconstruction already solves) and colour; the preset format; how presets are evaluated across scenes and turned into recipes.
  10. The UI's 3D stack — leaning: one three.js scene (section 9). Open: which splat renderer, and the LOD format for large clouds.
  11. Capture advice — leaning: layered (section 9). Open: how a viewpoint is computed (next-best-view method) and the actor profiles' shape.
  12. Rented workers: which providers first (GPU marketplaces, hyperscaler spot, European hosts), Terraform or OpenTofu, and how data reaches them — from home over the uplink, or staged in object storage near them.
  13. When renting pays: the job size and stage mix where a rented GPU beats the homelab after upload time and cost — a number RC-P7 can measure with one rented worker.
  14. Recipe selection: which evidence drives the proposal (EXIF/XMP, image count, sequence, priors, a tagged capture type), and how confident it must be before choosing without asking.
  15. The benchmark set: which captures, how reference dimensions are measured, which metrics gate a recipe change, and where the set lives (it holds private photos).
  16. A portable dense path for Macs (Metal or CPU), or dense always on a CUDA/HIP worker.
  17. The field split (owner, 2026-11-27): which stages run on the laptop before anything is sent, what leaves it (RAW, developed images at a working resolution, features, a sparse model), and what a field uplink allows; 1,500 photos at 50 MB are 75 GB.
  18. The field client (owner, 2026-11-27): a web application, a local client, or both; the laptop already runs the coordinator and a worker alone when offline (section 4), so the open part is how that is packaged and shown. Decided (owner, 2026-11-27): the Studio, the web application and the local engine packaged in Electron for macOS and Windows.

docs.title: Recce — Project Brief
docs.text:
Seed document for the concept package. Input to the Step 0 prototypes and to RC-01 Vision.

Version: 0.1 · Draft Prefix: RC Name: Recce (chosen 2026-11-24; formerly the working name "photogrammetry") Date: 2026-11-23 Inputs: landscape research · robotics-lab contract · hardware and parallelism

docs.title: 0. Where this comes from
docs.text:
Two things drive the project, in this order.

The robotics lab. The owner's robots map an apartment and will soon carry RGB and depth cameras. They know where they are, they can drive to viewpoints, and they need a model they can place back into their map — at a known scale, in a known frame, with an honest statement of what it does not know. Nothing open offers that as a service a robot or an agent can drive.

A talk at a diving conference. A photogrammetrist described buying a workstation of around €20,000 because 1,500 Nikon D850 photos of an underwater site would not assemble into a model on an M3 Pro laptop in the course of a day (the software was most likely Metashape). That is the problem in one sentence: large underwater sets of high-resolution RAW photos need compute that one laptop does not have, and today the answer is to buy one very expensive machine. The owner already has several capable machines, and a rented GPU for one night costs a fraction of that workstation.

Not satisfied with "it looks okay". The owner is evaluating the existing tools in parallel and is not happy with their outputs. Common practice is to load photos into Metashape, run a few basic steps and accept what comes out. This project goes into the matter instead: understand each step, measure what is wrong, and see how far a few weeks of focused work with AI coding agents can push the quality. The first horizon is weeks, not a product roadmap.

What the owner finds wrong in current outputs — all of it: blurry or smeared textures, noisy or melted geometry, holes, colour seams, wrong colour underwater, a scale that cannot be trusted, and slow processing. Each becomes a measurement before it becomes a fix:

Complaint What the engine measures Blurry, smeared textures Per-image sharpness at ingest; texture resolution per surface area; which images each texel blends Noisy or melted geometry Depth-map consistency across views; point density and noise against the benchmark objects Holes Coverage per region; which regions no image sees well enough Colour seams Exposure and white-balance spread across the set; seam contrast in the texture Wrong colour underwater Colour against a reference target in the scene; range-dependent attenuation estimate Untrustworthy scale Scale state on every product; error against measured distances (scale bars, tags) Slow Wall-clock time per stage and per machine, transfer time, cost per run

Data comes when the software is ready for it. The owner shoots the use-case sets (objects, room, car, bikes) once the first engine can take them, and asks a friend for a large dive set, with the friend's Metashape result as the baseline, in that same initial phase. Until then the engine is developed against public datasets with published ground truth (candidates to check for licence and fit: COLMAP's sample scenes, ETH3D, Tanks and Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, and the public underwater sets published with Sea-thru and SeaThru-NeRF).

Two horizons. The project is shaped for where it should be, not only for its next step.

  • In six months: three equal pillars. All the hardware as one pool, rented GPUs included; robots and agents as first-class clients; a photographer's tool from RAW to model, from Lego to reefs. No pillar is subordinate.
  • In the first month: three starting points. Small objects (the learning path where the engine is built and measured), underwater sites (the case that exposes the compute and quality problem), and robots (the first real client). The car, the bikes and the rest of the use cases follow once those three work.

Vision sentence under consideration (from the 2026-11-23 review): "A reconstruction engine that always says what it knows and what it does not — scale, frame, coverage, uncertainty — so that a person, a robot or an agent can decide what to capture next, above water and below." The vision as written after Step 0 is in RC-01 Vision (2026-11-27).

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
A self-hosted photogrammetry system that turns photographs into 3D models — meshes, point clouds and gaussian splats — using every machine its owner has. It is one engine with three ways in:

A web interface for people. Drop in photos from an iPhone, a GoPro, a DSLR or a drone; watch the reconstruction build; inspect, compare and export the result.

An HTTP API and a command line for programs. Robots, scripts and other projects submit capture sets — often with camera poses and intrinsics already known — and receive a model with a stated scale, frame and provenance.

An MCP server for agents. An agent starts and steers reconstructions, reads their quality state (what registered, what didn't, where coverage is thin), compares variants and says what to capture next.

RAW in, no detour. Photos arrive straight off the camera — NEF, ARW, ProRAW DNG, HEIC, GoPro JPEG or video — without a pass through Lightroom. A simple but good-enough imaging pipeline at the front (decode, white balance, exposure and tonality matched across the whole set) makes the photos agree with each other before they are stitched, so the model's colour and light hold together.

Underneath sits a coordinator and a pool of workers. A worker runs on any machine — Apple silicon, an NVIDIA ARM64 box, an AMD Linux box, a rented cloud GPU — and advertises what it can do. The coordinator splits a reconstruction into stages and pieces and places each one where it runs best. The laptop alone runs the system end to end as far as its hardware allows: ingest, develop, registration and a splat (Brush on Metal) today; dense depth and meshing need a CUDA or HIP worker until a portable dense path exists (an open question). More machines make it faster and complete, not different. When a job outgrows the homelab, rented cloud GPUs join the same pool — declared as infrastructure as code, started with the owner's go, gone when the job ends.

docs.title: 2. Who it is for
docs.text: Built first for one person: a photographer and underwater photographer with an iPhone 15 Pro, a GoPro, a Nikon D850, a Sony Alpha 1, a DJI Mini 4 Pro, and a homelab of heterogeneous machines. Built equally for that person's robots, which map an apartment and hand over well-posed capture sets through a file contract. And built for agents, which are a first-class client rather than an afterthought.

docs.title: What gets scanned
docs.text:
The range is wide on purpose, and it is the main design pressure:

Scale Examples Typical capture Small Lego toys, small parts, things around the house iPhone, DSLR, turntable Medium Mountain bike, motorbike, car iPhone, DSLR walk-around Interior The house from inside, room by room iPhone (LiDAR, ARKit), robots Large outdoor A whole building DJI Mini 4 Pro, DSLR Underwater Wrecks, reefs GoPro, DSLR in housing

One use case cuts across scales: realistic assets for game engines — a model clean enough (textured, sized, sensible polygon count) to drop into a game engine, as some phone apps do today.

docs.title: A phone capture app
docs.text: A small internal iPhone app that captures and sends straight to the system — no manual upload — and carries what a web page can't reach: LiDAR depth and ARKit camera poses, written in the same capture-set format the robots use (prototype RC-P11). Photos-only captures still come in through the web interface.

docs.title: The engine at the centre
docs.text:
The project is an engine first. At its centre is one structured, scientific model of a reconstruction: cameras and their calibration, images and their poses, matches and tracks, the sparse and dense geometry, the mesh and the splat — each with its units, its frame, its uncertainty and the step that produced it. Getting that geometry right is the work; everything else is built around it.

The web interface, the HTTP API, the command line and the MCP server are faces on that engine, not products of their own. The principle carries over from robotics-lab's Observatory: agent first, human friendly — anything a page shows is something a command answers, and the reverse. The coordinate frame and the scale are never hidden.

AI is optional; the product is complete without it (owner, 2026-11-27). Every view, check, quality report, readiness verdict, gap list and suggested shot works from geometry and rules alone, and is good enough on its own: the version without AI is not a placeholder. AI comes in two ways, both opt-in. First, Recce is an MCP server, so a person's own agent can drive it from outside. Second, a person brings their own AI into Recce: an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (a hosted provider such as OpenAI or Anthropic with their key, or a local model) set once in the settings. With it connected, features inside Recce go further: the run is explained in words, assessments and plans are written over the rule-based ones, and an agent places labels and shots in the scene. What the AI adds is marked as written by AI and checked against the engine's own numbers; the engine, not the AI, supplies positions and verdicts. The AI's role is a coach to the operator (owner, 2026-11-27): it says why a result is the way it is and how to get to a better one, as a plan built only from actions the engine can carry out (re-run with another option, re-shoot here, add a target), with how the operator will know it worked. Without AI, a rule writes the same kind of plan from the same facts.

Two registers in one interface (owner, 2026-11-24). The frame — panels, lists, inspectors, settings, the timeline of a run — is a professional tool in the family of Lightroom, Autodesk's products, Blender and Rerun, and follows robotics-lab's look (its Observatory and Mission Control: dark by default, an outliner, a read-only inspector, label-left and value-right in mono, shared design tokens). The 3D scene and everything that explains a reconstruction is where the project sets out to be different: illustrative, not technical; beautiful at every step, not only at the end; explaining what the engine did and why, with imagery good enough to show to someone who does not know the field. Existing tools present photogrammetry as a technical process that ends in a mediocre model; this one shows each stage as something to look at and understand — the cameras finding each other, the matches that hold the model together, where coverage is thin, what a recipe changed. The geometry and the rules carry this on their own; with AI connected, agents and multimodal models take it further: an agent can look at the intermediate products, describe them and point at what matters. Beauty here is not decoration: the interface is the connection between a person and the machine, and software that looks right is simpler and more intuitive, which is what makes a complex concept understandable. That is why the 3D scenes and the explanations carry so much weight. Inspiration reaches past Rerun, Blender and Foxglove to the most refined professional and explanatory software: colour and finishing tools such as DaVinci Resolve, design tools such as Figma and Linear, 3D tools such as Cinema 4D and Spline, and explanatory work such as Bartosz Ciechanowski's interactive articles and NASA's Eyes on the Solar System. The owner's taste drives this register; the agent's part is to propose boldly, build quickly to look at, and take critique. The design system (RC-05) and the UX specs carry the detail.

Upload and it lines up. The heart of the engine is registration: a thousand unordered photos of a wreck go in, and the engine finds features, chooses which photos to compare, verifies matches against two-view geometry, builds a view graph, solves every camera's position and refines the whole by bundle adjustment — calibrating the lenses as it goes, across mixed cameras. It rejects what doesn't fit with a stated reason, and when a capture falls apart into separate pieces it says where the link is missing instead of failing silently.

Strategies, not one pipeline. Each stage is a contract with several implementations — global (GLOMAP) and incremental (COLMAP) pose solving, a learned first pass, later a refractive camera model. Named recipes bundle the right choices for a capture type (turntable object, walk-around, interior, aerial, underwater, robot); the engine proposes one from the evidence and says why, and falls back when a stage underperforms. Control comes in three levels — automatic, recipe, expert. The owner's own captures, with measured reference dimensions, form a benchmark set that turns "this strategy is better for reefs" from opinion into a table.

docs.title: 3. What makes it different
docs.text:
It uses all the hardware. Distribution exists elsewhere — WebODM schedules onto many nodes, Meshroom runs on a render farm, Metashape Professional has network processing over shared storage, Brush trains splats on Metal and Vulkan — but none places stages by capability across CUDA, Metal and HIP machines that come and go, with rented GPUs joining for a night. This system treats a laptop, a GPU box and an idle desktop as one pool, across CUDA, Metal and HIP, with workers that join and leave.

Parallelism in every form. Per-image and per-pair fan-out, spatial partitioning of large scenes, a streaming pipeline that starts while photos are still uploading, and comparative runs of different pipelines side by side.

Known poses are first-class. Most tools estimate everything from pixels. Here a robot's poses, an iPhone's ARKit track or a drone's GPS are priors the pipeline uses, refines and reports on — and the result states its scale and frame, or says plainly that the scale is arbitrary.

Quality is visible, not implied. Registration, reprojection error, coverage and the differences between pipelines are state the UI shows and an agent can read — not a log file behind a "done" flag.

It explains as it goes. Every stage has a picture worth looking at, not only the final model: the reconstruction is shown as a story of how it was made, with the evidence for each claim on screen. The 3D presentation is designed, not a default viewer with a grid.

Underwater is a first-class case. Refraction, colour loss with depth, backscatter and moving subjects are the conditions the owner shoots in, not an edge case to ignore.

Against the reference. Agisoft Metashape is the industry reference: mature, accurate, $3,499 for the Professional edition with network processing. Its distribution splits work per task onto workers sharing one storage path; it documents CUDA and OpenCL but not Metal; and its 2.3 release trains no gaussian splats and models no underwater refraction (research). Those four gaps are this project's openings.

Pending: the minimal feature set — table stakes versus differentiators — is drafted in the product feature analysis §6 and decided in the interview. Agreed so far: splats are in the MVP, bounded.

docs.title: 4. Scope boundary
docs.text: A reconstruction tool: photographs and poses in, models with provenance out.

docs.title: Non-goals for the concept phase
docs.text:
• Capture control of robots and drones. They capture with their own software (the internal iPhone app records a capture set; it does not steer anything); this system states what a good capture needs and judges a capture after the fact.
  • Navigation-grade or survey-grade output. A pleasing model is not collision-safe and not a survey; models carry their scale and uncertainty, and say what they are not.
  • A cloud service, accounts or multi-tenancy. One owner, their machines, their data.
  • Model weights or tools under non-commercial licences in the default stack. They may be optional and are labelled where used.
  • Robotics code. The robot seam is files and a command line; nothing from robotics-lab is imported.

docs.title: Name and terminology (owner, 2026-11-24)
docs.text:
The project is Recce: short for reconnaissance, the survey that goes ahead of a mission. It fits the robots doing autonomous mapping runs and the drones surveying terrain, and works as a verb for anyone ("recce the wreck"). The theme stays light inside the product, which has to be plain to anyone who knows the field:

  • Domain terms come first and stay primary: capture set, reconstruction, camera pose, point cloud, mesh, splat, scale, frame, coverage, quality report, gap list.
  • A few mission words are allowed, always beside the standard term, never instead of it: a capture run may be called a sortie, the quality report a debrief, the gap list a brief for the next sortie. A screen title or a doc heading uses the standard term; the mission word is a secondary label at most.
  • No military vocabulary beyond these. No ranks, no callsigns, no "intel", no "targets" in the user-facing text (the gap-list data field targets is a technical name, not a label).
  • The engine package and command stay recon, as agreed in the robotics-lab contract.

docs.title: Settled in the interview (2026-11-23)
docs.text:
• Three pillars, equal — the six-month shape. All the hardware as one pool; robots and agents as first-class clients; a photographer's tool from RAW to model. No pillar is subordinate. The first month starts from small objects, underwater sites and robots (§0, Two horizons).
  • The iMac Pro is out (2026-11-24). The design and the prototypes use the M4 Pro, the X3, the GB10 and rented GPUs.
  • Storage stays conservative (2026-11-24). Keep what cannot be recomputed, evict what can, and add external disks to a machine when space runs short; the rule is in the architecture sketch §8.
  • The X3 is home. The coordinator runs on the X3, always on. The laptop is a client and a worker, and runs the whole system alone when offline in the field.
  • RAW pipeline: prototype both. A minimal own pipeline (rawpy/LibRaw, set-wide white balance, exposure and tone) and darktable driven from its command line are compared in RC-P5.
  • The iPhone app starts in Step 0 (revised 2026-11-23; first answer was "a later surface"). An internal capture app, installed on the owner's iPhone, records photos with ARKit poses, intrinsics and LiDAR depth and sends them to the engine. It writes the same capture-set format as robotics-lab's robots, so the phone and the robots share one ingest path. Web upload stays for photos-only captures.
  • Open source from the start, MIT (decided 2026-11-24; first answer was "open source later"). The default stack stays permissive (BSD, MIT, Apache). Copyleft tools run only as external processes, restricted weights are never shipped, and no dataset lives in the repository — the rules are in Licensing.
  • Assets land in Unreal Engine, Unity, Godot and Blender. All four are targets for the game-engine use case.
  • First scans, easiest to hardest: a matte household object (clean baseline), a Lego model (fine detail, turntable, masking), a room (ARKit and LiDAR priors, low-texture walls), the mountain bike (thin tubes, spokes, shiny parts).

  • Engine language: Python first, Rust kept open. Prototypes and the first engine are Python, next to the field's tooling (pycolmap, PyTorch, gsplat, rawpy). The data model is language-neutral from day one — a documented on-disk schema and a coordinator–worker wire protocol — so the coordinator or a worker agent can move to Rust where measurement says so. The question stays open in RC-04 and closes on the evidence from RC-P1, RC-P2 and RC-P7.

  • Architecture leanings (own pull-based worker protocol; one three.js scene; layered capture advice; splats in the MVP, bounded) are recorded in the architecture sketch §9, for the prototypes to confirm.

  • One monorepo. Engine, workers, web UI, the iPhone app (apps/ios/) and infrastructure as code live in this repository. Robotics-lab stays separate, joined by the capture-set format.

  • The first case: the owner's home, captured with the iPhone app (owner, 2026-11-27). The build starts with the iPhone capture app (RC-P11) and the owner photographing at home, from simpler to more complex: objects first, then a whole room. The room is the setting the robots map, so it leads into the robot use cases.

  • Learn mode is a feature inside the product (owner, 2026-11-27): the mini-labs and their tutor (RC-M5) live in Recce beside what they explain, not as a separate face.

  • Distribution is at the front, for work in the field (owner, 2026-11-27). The owner travels with a laptop and shoots with a camera, a drone or an underwater camera, and processes the day's work after. The answer is not a stronger laptop but offloading: the laptop sends work to the owner's other machines and to rented GPUs. Running workloads on other machines, rented GPUs included, is built from the beginning and is a key part of the vision, not a later scaling step. Open problems this raises: the upload (1,500 photos at 50 MB are 75 GB), whether the RAW files need to leave the laptop at all, and how work splits between the laptop and the remote workers before anything is sent.

  • Develop is its own module (owner, 2026-11-27): RAW decoding, lens correction and adjustments (white balance, exposure, tone, colour across the set), a mini Lightroom for reconstruction. It stands alone so it can be experimented on and prototyped by itself, it reuses third-party libraries as far as possible, and it has a develop panel where a person tunes and saves presets. Recce's own presets are learned by evaluation across scenes; together with the rest of a capture type's choices they form the recipes.

  • Workflows are the person's (owner, 2026-11-27): a project runs as a workflow, the chain of steps in the person's order (input, develop or not, preview, full pass, hand-over, pauses for review). People define their own, save several for different kinds of project, and change one during a mission; Recce proposes one, and a recipe fills in each step's settings.

  • Projects (owner, 2026-11-27): a project is the boundary of one scene and a container for its assets and its processing (workflow, develop settings, recipes, runs, models). Originals stay as files on disk in a folder per project, one subfolder per leg; Recce imports from a folder or a connected device, never modifies an original, switches projects in one step and exports or imports a project between computers. A small library and a photo viewer with the metadata sit inside the project; the darkroom works on groups of photographs that share their light, and matches the groups to each other.

  • Both: Recce Studio on the desktop, and the web (owner, 2026-11-27). The Studio is the web application packaged with the local engine in Electron, for macOS and Windows (Linux too); it does all RAW processing locally and sends only what the model needs. Recorded in RC-01.

docs.title: Open from the start
docs.text: Final name; implementation language and stack; how workers are deployed and secured on the tailnet; which mesh, point-cloud and splat formats; where photos live and how long.

docs.title: 5. Step 0 — Prototype plan
docs.text:
The hard parts here are computational and distributed; the architecture cannot be written honestly until they are proven. A prototype counts as proven when it meets its stated criterion — not when it looks plausible. A failure with its evidence is also a result.

Restructured 2026-11-24 after the advisor review: the platform matrix merged into the baseline; the iMac Pro dropped from the prototypes; distribution moved onto a large set with dense depth as its unit of work; quality state moved early with a hold-out test; every criterion made measurable. Development runs on public datasets until the owner's own captures and the friend's dive set arrive. Numeric tolerances were agreed with the owner on 2026-11-24.

Progress is kept in Step 0 status and findings; each prototype's README holds its numbers.

Old numbers → new: P1 and P2 → P1 · new P2 · P6 → P3 · new P4 · P7b → P5 · P7 → P6 · P3 → P7 · P4 → P8 · P5 → P9 · P9 → P10 · P10 → P11 · P8 → P12.

Two tracks, one meeting point (owner, 2026-11-24). Step 0 runs two tracks side by side. Below, the prototypes (RC-P1..P13) prove how the technology works. Above, the mock-ups (RC-M, in mockups/) work out how the product looks and behaves: every concept in the visual ideas catalogue is mocked, looked at and critiqued before anything is built. A mock-up is proven when the owner has judged it on screen and the concepts it carries are kept, changed or dropped with a reason. Mock-ups use real outputs from the prototypes wherever they exist (RC-P1's cameras and points first), so the picture shows real data, not invented data. The two tracks meet in the first build phase, where the PRDs, RFCs and UX specs draw on both, and the build starts from a worked-out design rather than discovering one.

docs.title: RC-P1 — Registration on every machine
docs.text: Proves: The registration core end to end on real photos, which machine runs it, and where the time goes. Input: ETH3D high-resolution training scenes (DSLR, 6048×4032, laser-scanned ground truth and ground-truth poses; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Proven when: GLOMAP and COLMAP each register at least two ETH3D scenes from the same verified matches on the M4 Pro, the X3 and the GB10; each machine × stage cell is pass, fail or CPU fallback, backed by a command and its output; per strategy, the record holds registration rate, reprojection error (mean and 95th percentile), wall-clock time per stage, and pose error against ETH3D's ground truth after Sim(3) alignment (rotation in degrees, position as a fraction of the scene's extent).

docs.title: RC-P2 — The expensive stages on the GPUs
docs.text: Proves: The two platform facts the hardware pillar rests on. Proven when: COLMAP's dense depth runs on one ETH3D scene on the X3 through a HIP build (gfx1151) and on the GB10 through CUDA, and gsplat trains a splat on the GB10 — or each failure is recorded with the error and what was tried. The GB10's available CUDA time under its shared-GPU schedule is recorded. If neither GPU path works, the rented GPU becomes the planned CUDA worker and the architecture sketch says so.

docs.title: RC-P3 — Quality state an agent can read
docs.text: Proves: That the engine's quality state is enough for an agent to find a real weakness. Proven when: quality.json v0 (registration rate, connected components, per-image verdict and reason, reprojection mean and tail, coverage per region, scale state) is produced from RC-P1 and served through three MCP read tools; then a hold-out test: all images seeing one region of an ETH3D scene are removed, the region's coverage metric drops by at least half (agreed 2026-11-24), an agent with only the MCP tools names that region among the scene's regions, and when the images return the metric recovers.

docs.title: RC-P4 — Dense, mesh, texture and splat, measured
docs.text: Proves: That the products are measurably good, not just plausible. Input: ETH3D evaluation scans; Mip-NeRF 360 for splats. Proven when: Dense cloud and mesh are scored against ETH3D's laser scans for accuracy, completeness and F-score at ETH3D's evaluation thresholds (1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 cm, with the BSD-licensed ETH3D multi-view-evaluation tool); the textured mesh and the splat come from the same poses; the splat's PSNR and SSIM on held-out views of at least two Mip-NeRF 360 scenes are recorded; the seven complaint measurements of §0 each have a first number.

docs.title: RC-P5 — RAW to a consistent set
docs.text: Proves: That a develop stage replaces the Lightroom step without hurting reconstruction, and which develop route to use. Input: ETH3D's NEF RAW files (the only public RAW set with laser ground truth found). Proven when: Three routes — the dataset's own JPEGs, a minimal own pipeline (rawpy, set-wide white balance and exposure), and Chemigram/darktable through its command line — each reconstruct the same scene; registration rate from RAW is no worse than from JPEG; the exposure and white-balance spread across the set and the seam contrast in the texture are measured for each; one route is chosen on those numbers.

docs.title: RC-P6 — Mesh and splat in the browser
docs.text: Proves: That one three.js scene shows the mesh and the splat together, on the laptop and the iPhone. Proven when: A RC-P4 mesh and a splat of about one million gaussians load together in one three.js scene from the result's files, render at 60 fps or more on the M4 Pro and 30 fps or more on the iPhone 15 Pro (agreed 2026-11-24), and the same result also exports to Rerun as the engineering view.

docs.title: C — Scale: the reason the project exists
RC-P7 — Distribution on a large set
docs.text: Proves: The central bet — that splitting the expensive work across machines, including a rented GPU, beats the best single machine after transfer costs. Input: COLMAP's Graham Hall (1,273 images) as the public stand-in; the friend's dive set when it arrives. Proven when: Dense depth per view runs split across the GB10, the X3 and one rented GPU, and the registration is cut into clusters solved on different machines and merged; the merged poses match a single-machine run within 0.1° rotation and 0.1% of the scene's extent in position, and dense depth maps match within 1% median relative difference (agreed 2026-11-24); wall-clock time, transfer time and rental cost are recorded against the fastest single machine. If splitting does not pay, the set size at which it would is the number recorded. Deferred to the build phase (owner, 2026-11-26): important, but not piloted in Step 0.

docs.title: RC-P8 — Learned and classical, compared
docs.text: Proves: Whether MapAnything's Apache checkpoint is a useful first pass — fast poses and metric scale — checked by bundle adjustment. Input: ETH3D (ground-truth poses); ARKitScenes (iPhone ARKit poses and LiDAR; non-commercial, development only). Proven when: On both, with and without pose priors, the learned-then-bundle-adjust route and the classical routes are compared on registration rate, pose error against ground truth, and scale error; the result decides whether the learned first pass enters a recipe.

docs.title: RC-P9 — A robot's capture set
docs.text: Proves: The file contract and metric placement. Input: An own fixture first — a Blender render of a room with exact camera poses, written in the capture-set format; a Gazebo set from robotics-lab when it exists. Proven when: recon reads the set, writes a model and provenance.json, and with exact poses the model's scale error is under 0.5% and its placement error under 1% of the scene's extent in the given frame (agreed 2026-11-24); the frame conversions (axes, handedness, camera-to-world) are checked by the render's known geometry.

docs.title: RC-P10 — A room from inside
docs.text: Proves: That an interior registers as one model, and what LiDAR and ARKit add. Input: ARKitScenes first; the owner's room later (use cases UC-B1). Proven when: With poses and depth, the room gives one metric model (TSDF mesh plus splat) whose wall lengths match the reference within 2% or 2 cm, whichever is larger (agreed 2026-11-24); photos-only, the room either registers as one model or the engine reports its separate components and where the links are missing.

docs.title: RC-P11 — The iPhone capture app
docs.text: Proves: That a small internal app captures what the Camera app cannot — ARKit poses, intrinsics and LiDAR depth with each photo — in the shared capture-set format. Timebox: one week (agreed 2026-11-24); it starts once RC-P8 or RC-P10 shows that pose priors improve the result. Proven when: The app writes a capture set that the engine's ingest reads unchanged, alongside a RC-P9 robot set; per-frame intrinsics, the image format and the ARKit-to-capture-set axis conversion are in the format (amendments proposed to robotics-lab); photos are at the highest resolution ARKit allows while tracking (to verify).

docs.title: RC-P12 — Underwater
docs.text: Proves: That the pipeline holds up underwater, and what refraction modelling and range-based colour correction add. Input: AquaMVS (lab refraction tests with a ChArUco board; CC BY 4.0) and SQUID (RAW with distance maps; non-commercial); SeaThru-NeRF scenes for splats. Proven when: On AquaMVS, distances between board corners are measured with the standard camera model and with a refractive model, and the error of each is recorded; on SQUID, range-based colour correction with ranges from the reconstruction is compared with uncorrected images on the scene's reference targets (identical DGK Color Tools charts placed at several distances); the open underwater benchmark is specified from what the public sets lack. The "ranges from the reconstruction" part moved to the open benchmark's site scene S1 (owner, 2026-11-26): on SQUID it cannot be met, and Step 0 does not test it.

docs.title: F — Structured models (added by the owner, 2026-11-26)
RC-P13 — A structured model from a reconstruction
docs.text: Proves: That an agent can turn a reconstruction and a little context (a few photos, one line of description) into a structured model (walls and rooms, passages, terrain and buildings) in which every element states whether it is measured, inferred or unknown, and how sure it is. The model is written once in a tool-neutral description; Blender, driven headless by the agent, is the first tool to build it, and others can follow against the same description. Input: three segments. Interior: RC-P10's room with the Faro scan (ARKitScenes). Cave from inside: a public cave set with a laser or survey reference, to be chosen. Drone over ground: EuroSDR RPAS Phase 2, Phantom 4 RTK (CC BY 4.0), with RTK positions and ground control. Proven when: In each segment the agent builds the structured model through the tool-neutral description, every element carries a source and an uncertainty, nothing tagged measured lacks support in the reconstruction, and the measured dimensions meet the segment's reference: room walls and floor area within 2% or 2 cm of the Faro scan; cave passage widths and heights against the set's reference, tolerance set when the set is chosen; drone terrain heights and building footprints against the control points. The number of agent iterations and where they went wrong is recorded.

docs.title: After Step 0 — the owner's data
docs.text: When the engine takes captures end to end, the owner shoots the use-case sets (use cases) and asks the friend for the dive set, with its Metashape result as the baseline. Both join the benchmark set.

docs.title: 6. Sequence after Step 0
docs.text: Prototypes and mock-ups → RC-01 Vision → RC-03 Data Catalog → RC-04 Technical Architecture → RC-05 Design System → RC-02 Project Concept → RC-00 Introduction → audit → PDF.

docs.title: First use cases — a thought experiment
docs.text:
Working document. The owner's first real scans, walked through the architecture sketch one by one, as a conceptual proof: does the shape hold, what breaks, which options and recipes each case needs. Input to the prototypes, to RC-02 and to RC-04.

Version: 0.1 · Draft · 2026-11-23

Device facts marked (to verify) come from general knowledge and were not checked against a source this session; the prototypes check them on the real devices.

docs.title: 1. The cases
docs.text:
The owner works through the same subjects with each device, in this order:

# Subject iPhone 15 Pro GoPro Nikon D850 Sony A1 A Object — a Lego toy, a camera, a book, a pair of shoes UC-A1 UC-A2 UC-A3 UC-A4 B Room — the owner's room, from inside UC-B1 UC-B2 UC-B3 UC-B4 C Car — in a car park, outdoors UC-C1 (any device) D Motorbikes (two) UC-D1 (any device) E Mountain bike UC-E1 (any device)

Cases A and B are the systematic series: one subject, four devices, so every device is compared on the same ground. C, D and E come along the way, with whichever device is at hand, and push the engine to its limits.

docs.title: 2. The same journey, step by step
docs.text:
Every case follows the same eight steps through the architecture. UC-A1 walks them in full; the others describe only what differs.

  1. Capture — what the device records, and what the owner should do.
  2. Into the system — which face, which files, what the ingest stage reads.
  3. Recipe — what the engine proposes from the evidence, and why.
  4. Registration — how the photos line up, and what is likely to resist.
  5. Scale and frame — where metric scale comes from, or why it is arbitrary.
  6. Products — dense cloud, mesh, texture, splat.
  7. Export — what leaves, in which format, for which tool.
  8. Quality and advice — what the engine reports, and what it tells the owner to reshoot.

docs.title: UC-A1 · Object with the iPhone 15 Pro (the full walk-through)
docs.text:
The four objects are four different problems:

Object What it tests Expected difficulty Pair of shoes Matte, textured, closed shape Easy — the clean baseline Book Near-planar faces, sharp edges, thin pages; a flat cover is close to the degenerate planar case for two-view geometry Medium — needs views around the edges, not only of the covers Lego toy Small, glossy plastic, fine detail, repeated studs (repetitive texture fools matching) Medium to hard Camera Black body (little texture), glass lens (transparent and reflective), metal Hard — expect holes at the lens; the splat will look better than the mesh

1. Capture. What the iPhone offers, and what of it reaches the engine:

Source What it gives How the engine gets it Main camera, 48 MP sensor; the Camera app saves 24 MP HEIF by default, 48 MP only in HEIF Max, JPEG Max or RAW Max at 1× (verified 2026-11-24) HEIC or JPEG, or ProRAW DNG Web upload, or AirDrop to the laptop then upload EXIF Focal length, lens id, exposure, GPS Read at ingest Lens switching The Camera app switches to the ultra-wide for close subjects (macro); it can be turned off with the Auto Macro button or Settings > Camera > Macro Control (verified 2026-11-24) EXIF lens id per image — the engine groups images by lens and calibrates each separately LiDAR depth Low-resolution metric depth Not in plain Camera photos. Only through a capture app (Record3D, Polycam, Scaniverse) or our own capture app (RC-P11) ARKit camera poses Metric camera positions, gravity Same: only through a capture app's export Portrait-mode depth A depth map embedded in the HEIC (to verify) Possible at ingest, but portrait mode is not a capture mode for photogrammetry

The owner shoots 60–150 photos in two or three rings around the object at different heights, with overlap between neighbours, exposure and focus locked (long-press AE/AF lock), on a plain matte background, in diffuse light. The finding: the plain Camera app gives photos and EXIF only. The LiDAR and ARKit data the owner wants to reuse needs a capture app's export — which is exactly what the later iPhone app exists for. Until then there are two ways in: photos-only (Camera app) and pose-and-depth (a capture app's export).

2. Into the system. The owner opens the web UI on the phone and uploads. Risk: Safari may convert HEIC on upload: it transcodes a file whose type is not in the page's accept list (verified 2026-11-24), so the upload page lists HEIC and DNG explicitly; what the photo picker hands over is tested on the phone — acceptable for a first test, but the ingest stage records which happened. ProRAW DNG files come through the Files picker. A capture-app export comes in as a folder: images, intrinsics, poses, depth.

3. Recipe. Evidence: one device, 60–150 images, not sequential, no GPS worth trusting indoors, the owner tagged "object". The engine proposes object-walkaround: retrieval-plus- exhaustive pair selection (small set, so exhaustive is affordable), incremental COLMAP or GLOMAP (RC-P1 decides the default), automatic background mask. With a capture-app export, it proposes object-walkaround+priors: ARKit poses as priors, LiDAR depth as a dense-stage prior.

4. Registration. Shoes register cleanly. The book's covers alone would be near-degenerate; views of the spine and edges carry it. Lego studs produce repetitive matches; geometric verification rejects most of the false ones, and masks keep the background from dominating. The camera's glass returns false matches that move with the viewpoint; bundle adjustment marks those points as high-error, and they are filtered. What resists: the iPhone's per-photo processing (Smart HDR, Deep Fusion) tone-maps each photo differently, and ProRAW is captured together with that processing, so it is not radiometrically linear (verified 2026-11-24). Matching tolerates it; texturing does not — hence ProRAW and the develop stage.

5. Scale and frame. Photos-only: arbitrary scale, stated as such, unless the owner puts a marker (an AprilTag sheet) or a ruler in the scene, or enters one measured distance in the UI. With ARKit priors: metric from priors, in ARKit's gravity-aligned frame. The model's "up" is known from gravity (ARKit) or from the ground plane.

6. Products. Dense depth on the GB10 (CUDA) or the X3 (a HIP build, unproven); Poisson mesh; texture with exposure-matched images; a splat from the same poses (on the GB10 with gsplat, or with Brush on the laptop alone).

7. Export. GLB with textures (Blender, Godot, Unity, Unreal), USDZ (iPhone Quick Look), OBJ and PLY; the splat as GLB with KHR_gaussian_splatting and as PLY. Every export states units and up axis.

8. Quality and advice. Registered 142/150, with the reasons for the eight rejects (blur, too little overlap). Reprojection error per image. Coverage regions: "the underside of the shoe is not covered — turn it over and shoot one more ring, keeping the background"; "the lens of the camera is missing in the mesh; it is present in the splat."

Verdict. Works for shoes and the book; works with masks and care for Lego; the camera works as a splat and partially as a mesh. Options this case needs: lens grouping by EXIF; automatic background masks; a two-sided capture mode (object turned over between rings, merged as one model); a scale-entry tool; ProRAW through the develop stage.

docs.title: UC-A2 · Object with the GoPro
docs.text:
Differs from A1: - Lens. GoPro photos in Wide/HyperView are strongly distorted; HERO13 photos offer Wide (16–34 mm) and Linear (19–39 mm) only, and RAW (.gpr) requires Wide (verified 2026-11-24); Linear mode is dewarped in-camera to a near-pinhole image at some cost in field of view. The recipe differs: a fisheye camera model for Wide, pinhole for Linear. The engine reads the lens mode from metadata where it can (the GPMF spec defines field-of-view and projection tags; whether HERO13 photos write them is tested on a real file). - Close focus and resolution. The GoPro has fixed focus (minimum distance unpublished; measured on the camera); the Macro Lens Mod focuses at 11–75 cm and, like every lens mod, is calibrated as its own camera; a small Lego model fills little of the wide frame, so effective resolution on the object is low. Shoes and the book are better targets than Lego. - Capture. Time-lapse photo (a frame every 0.5 s) while walking around is the natural mode; video works but brings rolling shutter and motion blur. For video the frame-select stage picks sharp, well-spaced frames. - Metadata. GPMF carries gyro, accelerometer and gravity; gravity gives "up", and gyro could seed rotations (no evidence found yet of GPMF used as an SfM prior — an opening, not a given). - Into the system. SD card or USB to the laptop, then upload; Open GoPro over Wi-Fi later.

Verdict. Works for medium objects in Linear mode; Wide mode needs the fisheye model to be good; small objects are a poor fit. Options: fisheye camera model; frame selection for video and time-lapse; GPMF gravity as "up".

docs.title: UC-A3 / UC-A4 · Object with the Nikon D850 and the Sony A1
docs.text:
Differs from A1: - Files. NEF and ARW RAW, 45.7 MP and 50.1 MP, tens of MB each — 150 photos is several GB. LibRaw lists both cameras; whether the A1's compressed ARW variants decode correctly in rawpy is unverified (RC-P5). - Develop. This is the case the develop stage exists for: one white balance and one exposure across the set, a neutral tone curve, no per-photo look. Without it the texture shows seams. - Resolution pyramid. Matching at full 45–50 MP is slow and unnecessary; the engine extracts features at a reduced size and keeps full resolution for dense depth and texture. - Lens. A prime or a zoom fixed at one focal length; aperture f/5.6–f/8; a tripod or a fast shutter. The lens model from EXIF initialises calibration; a zoom moved mid-set splits the set into calibration groups, which the engine detects from EXIF focal length. - Turntable option. With a DSLR on a tripod and the object on a turntable, the background is static while the object turns. The background must be masked out or be featureless, or it pulls the solution towards "the camera never moved". This is the object-turntable recipe. - Scale. A printed AprilTag board beside the object gives metric scale and up.

Verdict. The best object quality of the four devices; the heaviest data; the strongest test of the develop stage and of distribution (feature extraction over hundreds of large images fans out well). Options: RAW develop; resolution pyramid; calibration groups by focal length; turntable recipe with static-background exclusion; marker-based scale.

docs.title: UC-B1 · Room with the iPhone 15 Pro
docs.text:
What makes a room different from an object: the camera is inside the subject looking out. Walls are often plain (little texture); windows and mirrors reflect; lighting is mixed (daylight and lamps); furniture occludes. And the classic mistake: standing in the middle and turning on the spot gives no parallax — pure rotation is the degenerate case, and nothing triangulates.

  • Capture. Walk along the walls, facing across the room, in overlapping passes at two heights; corners and doorways shot deliberately. Two modes:
  • Photos-only — the Camera app. Plain walls will resist registration.
  • Pose-and-depth — a capture app's export with ARKit poses and LiDAR depth. This is where the iPhone's extra sensors matter most: ARKit poses hold the solution together across plain walls, LiDAR depth gives geometry where photos have no texture, and the scale is metric.
  • Recipe. interior: sequential and retrieval pair selection, ARKit priors if present, the learned first pass (MapAnything) when texture is low, TSDF fusion from LiDAR depth alongside photo-based dense depth.
  • Registration. Photos-only: expect the room to break into pieces at plain walls; the engine reports the separate components and where the links are missing ("the wall between the window and the door has no overlap"). With priors: one model.
  • Scale and frame. Metric from ARKit, gravity-aligned; or one tape-measured wall length entered in the UI.
  • Products. A metric mesh for measuring and for robotics-lab comparisons; a splat for viewing, where a room looks far better than as a mesh.
  • Privacy. A room scan holds screens, documents and photos on walls; the project is marked "never leaves home" by default.

Verdict. Photos-only is the honest stress test and may fail at plain walls; pose-and-depth is expected to work and is the case for the capture-app route. Options: pose priors; depth fusion; learned first pass for low texture; component reporting; the default "stays home" for interiors.

docs.title: UC-B2 · Room with the GoPro
docs.text:
• The wide field of view helps a room: more overlap per frame, more texture in each image, fewer photos needed. The fisheye model is required.
  • Indoors the GoPro's small sensor raises noise and lengthens exposure; video blurs in low light. Time-lapse photo in good light, or video with plenty of light.
  • No depth, no poses; GPMF gravity gives "up". Scale arbitrary without a measured distance.

Verdict. Likely registers better than iPhone photos-only thanks to the field of view; detail is lower. Options: fisheye model; frame selection; low-light warnings at ingest (ISO and shutter read from EXIF).

docs.title: UC-B3 / UC-B4 · Room with the Nikon D850 and the Sony A1
docs.text:
• A wide lens (or the widest the owner has) and a tripod for low light; mixed light makes white balance across the set matter even more — the develop stage again.
  • Highest detail and the largest data; the case where distribution and rented workers start to matter.
  • No poses, no depth; scale from a tape measure or a marker on the wall.

Verdict. Works where there is texture; plain walls resist as with the iPhone photos-only. Options: as UC-B1 photos-only, plus RAW develop and tripod-aware capture advice.

docs.title: 5. Case C — a car in a car park
docs.text:
• Size and height. About 4.5 m long and 1.5 m high; the roof needs views from above — a step ladder, a pole, or the DJI Mini 4 Pro (a natural moment to bring the drone in).
  • Surfaces. Glossy paint and glass reflect the surroundings, and reflections move with the viewpoint: false matches, holes in the mesh. Overcast light is far better than sun; a polarising filter on the DSLR cuts reflections.
  • Outdoors. Other cars, people, moving shadows: masks and a moving-object filter. Sun moves over a long capture; exposure locked anyway.
  • Recipe. object-walkaround at large scale, or aerial for the roof pass when the drone is used, merged into one model through shared images.
  • Scale. The wheelbase from the car's specification, or a tape-measured distance; GPS (phone or drone) gives rough scale and north.
  • Products. The splat is the showpiece; the mesh is good on matte parts (tyres, trim) and holed on glass. Paint reconstructs if overcast.

Verdict. Works as a splat; works partially as a mesh; the drone pass is what makes the roof whole. Options: reflective-surface handling (masks, robust filtering); moving-object masks; multi-device merge (ground photos plus drone); scale from a known dimension.

docs.title: 6. Case D — the motorbikes
docs.text:
• Chrome, polished metal and black engine parts; thin cables and spokes; deep occlusions between engine, frame and wheels.
  • Capture in rings at several heights plus close passes into the engine bay; overcast light or a shaded garage.
  • The mesh struggles with thin and shiny parts; the splat handles them far better.
  • Two motorbikes: the same recipe twice — a first use of the benchmark idea across subjects.

Verdict. Splat good, mesh partial; a strong showcase for "same poses, two products". Options: splat as the primary product for this subject type; mesh cleanup; close-pass capture advice.

docs.title: 7. Case E — the mountain bike
docs.text:
• The hardest object: thin tubes, spokes, cables, and very little surface per view — most of each photo is background seen through the bike.
  • Masks are mandatory; a plain background (a wall, a sheet) makes them reliable. On a work stand, the bike can be turned like a turntable — the object-turntable recipe with static background exclusion.
  • The mesh of the spokes is expected to fail; the frame and wheels' rims work. The splat renders the spokes acceptably (expected, not verified).

Verdict. The stress test RC-P1's order puts last for a reason. Options: strong masking; turntable recipe; thin-structure handling is a later research item (mesh from splats).

docs.title: What holds
docs.text:
• The eight-step journey fits every case without a new component: ingest, recipe, registration, scale, products, export, quality and advice cover them all.
  • Recipes are necessary, not decoration. Within these first cases alone the engine needs at least object-walkaround, object-turntable, interior and aerial, each differing in pair selection, priors, masking and camera model.
  • Scale state earns its place. Half the cases end with arbitrary scale unless the owner adds a marker or a measurement; the engine must say so every time.
  • Same poses, two products pays off on exactly the owner's subjects: glass, chrome, spokes.

docs.title: What breaks, or needs care
docs.text: Problem Cases Answer in the design iPhone LiDAR and ARKit are not in Camera-app photos A1, B1 Two ingest routes: photos-only and pose-and-depth (capture-app export); the iPhone app later Per-photo processing in the iPhone (Smart HDR) A1, B1 ProRAW plus the develop stage; detect inconsistent tone across the set at ingest Automatic lens switching (macro) A1 Group by lens id from EXIF; calibrate per group; warn Safari HEIC to JPEG on upload A1, B1 Record what arrived; offer the Files route for originals Fisheye distortion A2, B2 Fisheye camera model in the recipe Rolling shutter and blur in video A2, B2 Frame selection; prefer time-lapse photos Repetitive texture (Lego studs) A1–A4 Geometric verification; masks; retrieval pairs Reflective and transparent surfaces A1 (camera), C, D Masks, robust filtering, splat as the faithful product Plain walls, pure rotation B1–B4 Pose priors, LiDAR depth, the learned first pass; capture advice ("move, don't turn") Static background on a turntable A3, A4, E object-turntable recipe with background exclusion Very large RAW sets A3, A4, B3, B4 Resolution pyramid; distribution; resumable upload Thin structures D, E Splat first; mesh-from-splat later Roof and top views C The drone; multi-device merge Moving people and cars outdoors C Moving-object masks

docs.title: Indoors against outdoors
docs.text: Concern Indoors Outdoors Light Low and mixed: noise, long exposures, white-balance mismatch Strong and moving: harsh shadows, specular highlights; overcast is best Background Static, often plain Busy and moving: people, cars, trees in wind Scale sources ARKit, LiDAR, tape, markers GPS (rough), known dimensions, markers, drone Typical recipe interior, object-turntable object-walkaround, aerial Privacy High (homes) — stays home by default Lower; rented workers allowed by default

docs.title: Engine capabilities this adds to the requirements
docs.text:
1. Two ingest routes for the iPhone: photos-only and pose-and-depth (capture-app exports first).
  2. Calibration groups by lens and focal length from EXIF.
  3. A fisheye camera model alongside the pinhole and Brown models.
  4. Frame selection for video and time-lapse.
  5. A resolution pyramid: features at reduced size, dense and texture at full size.
  6. Automatic background masks, and moving-object masks outdoors.
  7. Recipes: object-walkaround, object-turntable (static background exclusion), interior (priors, depth fusion, learned first pass), aerial; multi-device merge across them.
  8. Scale entry: markers (AprilTag boards), one measured distance, or a known dimension.
  9. Ingest checks: tone inconsistency across the set, HEIC transcoding, low-light warnings.
  10. Component reporting when a capture breaks into pieces, with where the link is missing.
  11. Per-project "stays home" defaults by capture type.

docs.title: Which prototype proves what
docs.text: Case Proven by UC-A1 shoes, book RC-P1 (baseline), RC-P8 (learned vs classical, with and without ARKit priors) UC-A1 Lego, camera RC-P1 extended; RC-P6 (splat vs mesh in the viewer) UC-A2 RC-P1 (fisheye model on every machine) UC-A3, UC-A4 RC-P5 (RAW develop), RC-P7 (distribution over large images) UC-B1 RC-P8 (priors), plus RC-P10 — a room from inside (TSDF from LiDAR, plain walls, components) UC-B2–B4 RC-P10 UC-C1, D1, E1 After Step 0 — the first real tests of the v1 recipes

docs.title: 9. The owner's kit and answers (2026-11-23)
docs.text:
• GoPro: HERO13 Black. (To verify: RAW photo (GPR) support and in which modes; lens modes available in photo and time-lapse; whether the HB-series lens mods — Macro, Ultra Wide — are worth testing for objects.)
  • Lenses: a wide range for both the D850 and the A1; the engine's recipes name what fits — a macro or short-tele prime around 90–105 mm at f/8–f/11 on the tripod for small objects (Lego, the camera), a normal prime around 35–50 mm for shoes, books and the motorbikes, a wide prime around 20–24 mm for the room and the car. One focal length per capture set.
  • Tripod: yes. Neutral background: yes. Turntable: improvised — the object-turntable recipe is tested from the start.
  • Markers and scale bars: acceptable in the first tests. A printed AprilTag board is the default scale and "up" source for object captures.
  • iPhone pose-and-depth route: the owner is ready to build an internal iPhone capture app now rather than depend on a third-party app. See RC-P11 in the brief.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Standing reference material that the concept documents and the code lean on.

  • Photogrammetry primer: the theory behind every stage.
  • Tools overview: libraries, models and formats, with licences.
  • Product feature analysis: what a complete product offers.
  • Public datasets: datasets for development, with ground truth and licences.

docs.title: Photogrammetry primer
docs.text: This document is the standing reference for the theory behind the engine. It exists so that the operator, who knows light, lenses and water better than linear algebra, and the coding agents, who know linear algebra better than reefs, share one vocabulary and one set of reasons. Every section explains the intuition first, then the maths, then states what the idea forces on the design. When a design question comes up, such as why a model must say whether its scale is metric, why a flat port breaks the pinhole model or why a splat is not a measurement, the answer starts here. Where this primer and the code disagree, one of them is wrong and the disagreement gets fixed, not tolerated.

docs.title: 1. What photogrammetry is
docs.text:
Photogrammetry recovers the shape of the world from photographs. A photograph throws away one dimension: every pixel records light that arrived along a ray, and nothing says how far along the ray the surface sat. A single image cannot give depth. Two images of the same point from different positions can, because the two rays cross at the point. Photogrammetry is the discipline of finding those crossings for millions of points at once, while also discovering where the cameras were and how their lenses bend light.

The difficulty is that nothing is known at the start. The camera positions are unknown, the point positions are unknown, and the only observations are pixel colours. The field's central trick is to solve everything together. If enough points are seen from enough views, the system of equations that ties points, cameras and pixel observations together has a unique answer, up to a small, well-understood ambiguity (section 6). The rest of the pipeline is engineering around that idea: finding which pixels in different photographs show the same point, solving for geometry robustly in the presence of wrong matches, then densifying and dressing the result.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
capture --> develop --> features --> matching --> SfM (poses + sparse points)
 (photos,    (RAW to     (keypoints,  (pairs,        |
  video,      matched     descriptors) verification) v
  poses)      images)                          bundle adjustment
                                                     |
                  +----------------------------------+
                  |                                  |
                  v                                  v
            dense MVS                        radiance-field branch
            (depth maps, fusion)             (NeRF, 3D gaussian splatting)
                  |                                  |
                  v                                  v
            surface (mesh)                       splat (.ply and kin)
                  |
                  v
            texture (UV, materials)

Each stage consumes the output of the one before and adds a kind of knowledge:

Stage Input Output Capture The scene Images, optionally poses, depth, GPS Develop RAW or camera JPEG Consistent, linear-light-aware images Features Images Keypoints with descriptors Matching Descriptors Verified image pairs with point correspondences SfM Correspondences Camera poses, intrinsics, sparse 3D points Bundle adjustment All of the above Jointly refined poses and points Dense MVS Posed images Per-view depth maps, a dense point cloud Surface Dense points or depth Triangle mesh Texture Mesh and posed images UV-mapped colour, materials Radiance field Posed images, sparse points A model that renders novel views

The radiance-field branch leaves the classical path after pose estimation. NeRF and 3D gaussian splatting do not build a surface; they fit a function or a cloud of translucent blobs so that rendering them from the known camera poses reproduces the photographs. They need the same poses the classical branch needs, which is why structure from motion stays at the centre of both.

docs.title: What this means for the engine
docs.text: The pipeline is a directed graph of stages whose outputs are typed artefacts, and the reconstruction data model holds every one of them with its units, frame and producing step. Poses are the hinge: both branches consume them, so pose quality is the first thing the engine measures and reports. Stages are separable, which is what lets the coordinator place feature extraction on one machine and dense stereo on another.

docs.title: The pinhole model
docs.text:
A camera maps a 3D point to a 2D pixel. The simplest faithful model is the pinhole: all light passes through one point, the centre of projection, and lands on an image plane behind it. A point at \((X, Y, Z)\) in the camera frame, with \(Z\) pointing forward along the optical axis, lands at

\[ x = f \frac{X}{Z}, \qquad y = f \frac{Y}{Z} \]

on the image plane. The division by \(Z\) is the whole story of perspective: distant things shrink, and a pixel fixes a direction but not a distance.

Two coordinate frames matter. The world frame is where the scene lives. The camera frame has its origin at the centre of projection, \(Z\) forward, \(X\) right, \(Y\) down in the computer-vision convention. A rigid transform takes world points to camera points:

\[ \mathbf{X}_c = R\,\mathbf{X}_w + \mathbf{t} \]

\(R\) is a \(3 \times 3\) rotation, \(\mathbf{t}\) a translation. These are the extrinsics, written \([R \mid \mathbf{t}]\). They are a world-to-camera transform. The camera's centre in world coordinates is \(\mathbf{C} = -R^\top \mathbf{t}\), and confusing \(\mathbf{t}\) with \(\mathbf{C}\) is a classic source of mirrored and displaced reconstructions. A pose handed to the engine by another system, a robot or ARKit, is often the opposite direction, camera-to-world, and the direction must be stated, never assumed.

docs.title: Intrinsics
docs.text:
The intrinsic matrix converts camera-frame rays to pixels:

\[ K = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & s & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = K \,[R \mid \mathbf{t}] \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_w \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

\(f_x, f_y\) are the focal length measured in pixels, \((c_x, c_y)\) is the principal point (where the optical axis meets the sensor, near the image centre but never exactly there), \(s\) is skew (zero for any modern sensor), and \(\lambda\) is the depth along the ray. Focal length in pixels, not millimetres, is what the geometry uses. Most pipelines set \(f_x = f_y\) and fit one focal length.

The camera is therefore described by six extrinsic numbers per image and a handful of intrinsics per lens. Photos taken with the same lens at the same focal setting share intrinsics, which is a powerful constraint: it lets one set of intrinsics be estimated from hundreds of images. A zoom lens or a lens that focuses by changing its internal geometry breaks the sharing, because its effective focal length changes with focus and zoom.

docs.title: Initial focal length from EXIF
docs.text:
Optimisation needs a starting value, and EXIF supplies one. If the image is \(W\) pixels wide and the sensor is \(S_w\) millimetres wide, a lens of focal length \(f_{mm}\) has

\[ f_{px} = f_{mm} \cdot \frac{W}{S_w} \]

When the sensor width is unknown but the 35 mm-equivalent focal length \(f_{35}\) is recorded, the same quantity follows from the 36 mm reference width: \(f_{px} = f_{35} \cdot W / 36\) for the long side. The EXIF value is approximate: lenses breathe with focus, manufacturers round, and crops and in-camera processing change the effective sensor area. It is a prior to refine, not a measurement. Phones and action cameras often report a focal length after in-camera distortion correction, which means the image no longer follows the lens's raw geometry.

docs.title: Lens distortion
docs.text:
Real lenses bend straight lines. The standard correction works in normalised coordinates \((x, y) = (X/Z, Y/Z)\) with \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\). The Brown–Conrady model applies radial and tangential terms:

\[ \begin{aligned} x_d &= x\,(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4 + k_3 r^6) + 2 p_1 x y + p_2 (r^2 + 2x^2) \\ y_d &= y\,(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4 + k_3 r^6) + p_1 (r^2 + 2y^2) + 2 p_2 x y \end{aligned} \]

The \(k_i\) are radial coefficients (barrel and pincushion), the \(p_i\) tangential coefficients (a lens element slightly off-axis). Pixels follow from \(u = f_x x_d + c_x\), \(v = f_y y_d + c_y\). The model is a polynomial in \(r\), which behaves well up to moderate field angles and fails for very wide lenses, because the true relation between angle and image radius is not a polynomial in \(\tan\theta\) and, at \(\theta \to 90^\circ\), \(\tan\theta\) diverges.

Fisheye models work with the angle \(\theta\) between the ray and the optical axis instead. The ideal equidistant projection is \(r = f\,\theta\): image radius grows linearly with angle, so a 180 degree field fits on a finite sensor. Real fisheye lenses deviate, and the OpenCV fisheye model, which follows the Kannala–Brandt form, adds a polynomial in \(\theta\):

\[ r_d = f\,\theta_d, \qquad \theta_d = \theta\,(1 + k_1 \theta^2 + k_2 \theta^4 + k_3 \theta^6 + k_4 \theta^8) \]

A GoPro in its wide modes is a fisheye in practice, and many of its "linear" modes are a software remap of a fisheye image. Using the wrong model leaves systematic residuals that the optimiser cannot absorb. Distortion parameters are estimated in the bundle adjustment, ideally from a set with strong geometry and a wide range of image positions for each feature, so that the edges of the frame are constrained.

docs.title: Rolling shutter
docs.text:
The pinhole model assumes the whole image is exposed in one instant. A global shutter does that. Most phones, action cameras and many mirrorless cameras in electronic-shutter mode use a rolling shutter, which exposes and reads rows one after another, so the top row and the bottom row see the world at times separated by roughly ten to thirty milliseconds, depending on the sensor. If the camera moves during that interval, each row has a slightly different pose, and the image is skewed, wobbled or bent: verticals lean in a pan, propellers bend.

For a still photo from a held phone the effect is small. For video it matters, because the camera is moving continuously by design and the frames are taken at speed. The geometry then holds only approximately: the rigid-camera model leaves residuals that grow with velocity, and a naive bundle adjustment either absorbs them as error or distorts the intrinsics to compensate. Mechanical shutters on DSLRs, such as the D850 in normal mode, are not subject to this in the same way. Electronic-shutter modes on mirrorless bodies, including the Alpha 1, read out row by row and carry the rolling-shutter effect to a degree that depends on sensor readout speed.

docs.title: What this means for the engine
