docs.title: 3.2 The fields
docs.text:
Top level.

  • gap_list is the integer schema version. A reader accepts its own and older versions and refuses a newer one, the rule robotics-lab already applies to manifest.json (RFC-0025 §5.1). Fields are only added within a version; a reader ignores fields and kind values it does not know.
  • id is content-addressed from the reconstruction, the ruleset and the thresholds. The same input gives the same id and the same list, as provenance.json promises.
  • capture_set echoes the manifest: id, manifest version, sha256, the source run_id, an optional site (proposal, section 6) and targets, the gap ids this capture set was taken for.
  • reconstruction names the strategy, recipe, engine version and the provenance.json it belongs to. Two strategies on one capture are two reconstructions and two gap lists (the RC-M1 mock-up shows GLOMAP and incremental side by side); a gap never moves between them.
  • ruleset names the thresholds that produced the list (gaps-1: 15 degrees median angle, 3 photos, and so on; the values are placeholders until RC-P3 measures them (inferred)).
  • purpose, rankings, complete_for: the list is ranked for all four purposes at once, so a consumer picks without a second call. complete_for is true when no gap of level major or above remains open for that purpose.
  • pose_convention states how a pose is read. It follows the manifest field proposed in capture-set amendments §3.

frame (critical).

  • name and id: the id changes whenever the frame's definition changes. A consumer compares it with its own frame identity before using a position.
  • axes: up is "+z" when the frame is gravity-aligned and null when it is not (a pure structure-from-motion frame has no known up).
  • units: "m" or "model".
  • scale_state: metric, metric-from-priors, scaled-by-markers or arbitrary (architecture sketch §2).
  • placement: whether the frame is registered to a named external frame. status is exact (priors with source: truth), estimated (priors with source: belief, with residual_rms_m, priors_used, priors_rejected) or none.

Each gap.

  • id: allocated by Recce per project, never reused, kept when a gap is matched across re-runs (status.matched_from names the earlier list and gap). Matching is by kind plus region overlap, or by photo id. A merge or split is recorded in the diff.
  • kind: thin_angle, few_photos, photo_not_joined, no_scale now; holes, blurred_photo, missing_colour_reference, disconnected_components later. scope says whether the gap lives in a region, a photo or the whole reconstruction.
  • severity: intrinsic to the evidence and the same for every purpose. level is critical, major, minor or info; score is 0 to 1; basis is a plain statement of the numbers behind it.
  • priority: rank and score per purpose. Purpose changes order and level of urgency, never the evidence. A no_scale gap is first for measurement and rank 5 for web viewing.
  • region: sphere (centre, radius) in the frame's units, or null where the location is unknown or does not apply.
  • evidence: points, photo ids, triangulation angle percentiles, a scale-free depth_rel_sigma (depth uncertainty as a fraction of range, valid in any frame), the coverage ring (azimuth bins; seen holds photo counts per bin; unseen_arcs_deg lists the empty arcs), observations per point, the solver's reason_code for a photo that did not join, and prior_pose where the image carried one (a robot's belief), which tells where the photo was probably taken.
  • close_when: the machine-checkable criterion the re-run evaluates. It travels with the gap so the consumer knows what "done" means before it plans.
  • viewpoints: see below.
  • landmark: the nearest existing photo, used to recognise the spot. It is a photo id; the image itself is served only to clients holding the image scope (section 6).
  • text: the human card (title, instruction, why). The same text feeds the web shot card, so humans and machines read one source.
  • hints: how much to capture: baseline_deg and baseline_m (metric only), photos min and target, overlap_min, capture_mode, and per kind extras such as retake_of or the scale reference kinds.
  • status: the lifecycle (section 3.4).

docs.title: 3.3 Viewpoints, and what a consumer may and may not do
docs.text:
A viewpoint is a candidate, never an order. Fields: pose (position, look_at, up; no quaternion is primary, because robotics-lab states no order for its quaternions (RFC-0025 §3.3, truth row); an optional quaternion_xyzw is named when present), planar ({x, y, yaw, frame} in the robotics-lab shape plus camera_height_m, present only when the frame is gravity-aligned and metric), relative (the viewpoint expressed from a landmark photo: orbit angles about the region centre and a distance ratio; scale-free), acceptance (an arc or annular sector, so a planner may pick any reachable point inside it), tolerance (position radius, a cone half-angle for the look-at direction, roll), and the gate: usable_as_goal with unusable_reason.

Recce knows no free space. The pose may lie inside a wall. The acceptance region is how a planner finds a reachable point; the planner checks reachability, no-go areas and clearances (RFC-0014 §3.4.8) itself.

Rules by frame state. usable_as_goal is computed by Recce from this table; a consumer reads the flag and does not re-derive it.

scale_state placement.status Consumer may Consumer may not arbitrary none Use kind, severity, priority, counts, evidence ratios, text, hints in counts and angles, the landmark photo, relative and its distance ratio. Show a human the card. Treat any position, radius, baseline or tolerance as metres; send pose or planar as a goal; write anything into a map; compare positions with its own frame. up is null: no heading from the model frame is a compass or gravity direction. scaled-by-markers none The above, plus metric sizes and distances inside the model. Place viewpoints in the robot frame: the frame is the markers', not the robot's. A consumer with its own alignment (three or more point pairs, a landmark photo with a known pose) may transform it; Recce does not vouch for the result. metric-from-priors estimated, frame id equal to the consumer's Use pose and planar as candidate goals after its own reachability check, and the tolerance as acceptance bounds. usable_as_goal is true only where residual_rms_m is under half the viewpoint's position_m. Skip the check against its map and guardrails; treat a viewpoint as collision-safe. metric-from-priors estimated, frame id different (another run's map) Use as scaled-by-markers above. Assume that two map frames match (RFC-0014 §3.5.4). metric or priors with source: truth exact As the row above estimated, with the tolerance at its tightest. Typical case: a simulator capture set. Treat truth as safe to drive.

The same rule in one line: Recce never turns a number into metres that the frame does not carry. When it cannot, it says so in unusable_reason (scale_state_arbitrary, frame_not_registered, frame_id_mismatch, residual_too_large, up_unknown).

A second, short example, the same gap in a robot capture set with exact priors (all values illustrative):

"frame": { "name": "map", "id": "frm-run-0042-map", "axes": {"handedness":"right","up":"+z","units":"m"},
           "scale_state": "metric-from-priors",
           "placement": { "status": "exact", "registered_to": {"name": "site", "id": "site-home"},
                          "residual_rms_m": 0.02, "priors_used": 212, "priors_rejected": 0 } },
"viewpoints": [ { "id": "vp-0007a", "role": "primary",
  "pose": { "position": [2.31,1.40,0.18], "look_at": [3.05,2.12,0.22], "up": [0,0,1] },
  "planar": { "x": 2.31, "y": 1.40, "yaw": 0.77, "camera_height_m": 0.18, "frame": "site" },
  "tolerance": { "position_m": 0.15, "look_at_cone_deg": 10, "roll_deg": 10 },
  "usable_as_goal": true, "unusable_reason": null } ]

A no_scale gap on a robot capture set is a contract failure, not a capture gap: the set promised priors, so the gap's evidence.priors_rejected names why the engine did not use them, and its severity for robot_localisation is critical.

docs.title: 3.4 The lifecycle
docs.text:
status.state moves as follows.

State Meaning Set by open Found, nobody has claimed it Recce, on computing planned A consumer has a plan for it: claims holds {client, plan_ref, until} The consumer, mark_gap_planned; until expires like a lock lease (RFC-0017 lease, inferred as a model) and the gap returns to open captured A capture set naming the gap in targets was ingested; the re-run is pending Recce, on ingest closed The re-run met close_when Recce still_open The re-run ran, the gap was targeted and close_when is not met; attempts increments and last_delta holds the change in evidence Recce dismissed The operator waived it, with a reason ("unreachable", "not needed") The operator only; an agent token cannot (as areas, mcp_server.py) superseded Merged into another gap by the matcher Recce

Several clients can claim one gap (a phone and a robot); claims are information, not locks, because a gap is not a safety resource. A gap not targeted by a capture keeps its state across a re-run if it still exists, and closes with closed_by: "incidental" if the new data met close_when anyway.

docs.title: 4. Faces: one verb list
docs.text:
One list of verbs; each face spells it in its own way. Reads are open to every client token; the writes noted below need the named scope.

Verb MCP tool HTTP (proposed prefix /api/v1) CLI list list_gaps(project, reconstruction?, purpose?, status?, kind?, min_severity?, since_seq?) GET /projects/{p}/gaps?... recon gaps list get get_gap(id) GET /gaps/{id} recon gaps get ID brief gap_brief(project, purpose, actor?, max_gaps?, frame_id?) POST /projects/{p}/gaps/brief recon gaps brief --purpose P --actor FILE card get_shot_card(id, format) (json, markdown, png) GET /gaps/{id}/card recon gaps card ID plan mark_gap_planned(ids, plan_ref, until?) (scope plan) POST /gaps/{id}/plan recon gaps plan ID --ref R release release_gap(ids) (scope plan) DELETE /gaps/{id}/plan recon gaps release ID dismiss not offered to agents POST /gaps/{id}/dismiss (scope operator) recon gaps dismiss ID --reason R diff get_gap_diff(from, to?) GET /gap-lists/{to}/diff?from= recon gaps diff A.json B.json watch watch_gaps(project, since_seq) (poll) and the resource subscription GET /events?since= (server-sent events) recon gaps watch export export_gap_list(id) GET /gap-lists/{id} recon gaps export, and gaps.json in every --out

Notes on each.

  • gap_brief is the machine form of a shot card list. Input: a purpose, an actor profile (kind phone, drone, ground-robot, arm; camera height_m, pitch_range_deg, fov_deg, min_standoff_m; a ground robot's profile is derivable from its cameras.json mount and robot file (inferred)), and optionally the consumer's frame_id. Output: the top max_gaps for that purpose, re-ranked, each with only the viewpoints the actor can reach in principle (camera height and pitch range checked, no map), planar filled for planar actors, a dropped list with the reason per omitted gap, and the same frame block. A consumer that skips gap_brief and reads list_gaps gets the full document.
  • mark_gap_planned is how the loop closes on the Recce side before capture. It records the client name from the token (the token is the identity, auth.py) and a plan_ref that is opaque to Recce, for example mc:goal-run/123.
  • get_gap_diff answers "what changed": per gap closed, still_open with delta, new, regressed, merged, and a targets_report (section 5, step 8).
  • Resources. The gap list is also an MCP resource: recon://projects/{p}/gaps (the latest list), recon://gap-lists/{id} and recon://gaps/{id}. A client that subscribes receives resource-updated notifications when a new list or a status change lands. The dependable path is the poll with since_seq: robotics-lab's own MCP server exposes tools only (inferred from mcp_server.py), and its event stream already uses numbered events with since and a gap event for a ring that no longer holds the missed ones (CONTRACT.md, The event stream). Recce copies that: events gap-list-ready, gap-status, gap-diff-ready, each with seq.
  • Shape of replies. Success is {"ok": true, ...}, failure {"ok": false, "error": {"code", "message"}}, with honest status codes: the robotics-lab envelope, so a client written for one speaks to the other (proposal).
  • Auth. Per-client bearer tokens, the token names the client; plan and release need scope plan; images (landmark photos) need scope images; dismiss needs operator. The MCP server is a client of the HTTP API with an allow-list of routes, as robotics-lab's is (mcp_server.py). Its transport is open (section 8).
  • File mode. recon --images D --manifest M --out O writes O/gaps.json with no server. --previous O1/gaps.json carries gap ids and lineage into the new list, so the loop works on files alone; statuses planned and dismissed need the server and do not exist in file mode.

docs.title: 5. The loop
docs.text:
1. Capture. A robot or phone writes a capture set. The manifest carries the frame, the pose priors (source: truth|belief) and, new, the frame identity and the site (capture-set amendments already add pose_convention; section 6 adds the rest).
  2. Reconstruct. recon or the API runs the stages and writes gaps.json beside provenance.json. The frame block carries the placement result.
  3. Fetch. The planner (an outside agent holding both the mission-control and a recon MCP server, or Mission Control's model job) calls gap_brief(project, purpose="robot_localisation", actor=<profile>, frame_id=<site frame id>).
  4. Check the frame. If every returned viewpoint has usable_as_goal: true, the planner proceeds. If not, it uses the qualitative parts only (text, relative, counts) and either asks the operator for a capture by hand or raises a scale gap to the operator. No guess substitutes for the flag.
  5. Transform and plan. The planner transforms into its goal frame: none when the frame ids match, else its own transform for that run, which Mission Control knows from the dock pose (start_pose, dock_pose: CONTRACT.md). It subtracts the camera mount to get a base pose (RFC-0025 §5), picks a reachable point inside acceptance, checks its map and guardrails, then creates a goal: today point {x, y, frame}, with no heading (robotics-lab answer a; RFC-0025's yaw line is stale), and capture_view once it exists. An agent's run goes to the simulator first (target: sim), and a real run needs the operator, so a gap list is rehearsed in Gazebo before it moves a real robot (RFC-0014 §3.4.2, mcp_server.py).
  6. Claim. The planner calls mark_gap_planned(ids, plan_ref="mc:goal-run/123").
  7. Execute and record. The robot reaches the stand pose, takes the burst (hints.photos, hints.baseline_deg) with locked settings, and the model job writes a new capture set with targets: [{"gap":"gap-0001","viewpoint":"vp-0001a","goal_run":123}] and the same site and frame identity.
  8. Re-run and report. Recce ingests the set into the same project and sets the targeted gaps to captured. The cached stages are reused, so only what the new photos touch re-runs (architecture sketch §3). It computes a new gap list with matched ids and a diff. The diff reports, per gap: closed, still_open with the evidence delta (for example median angle 6.1 to 11.8 degrees against 15 needed, so "one more photo from the far side"), new gaps the extra photos exposed, regressed gaps, and a targets_report per target: which new photos registered, viewpoint_hit (position_error, look_at_error_deg against the tolerance), and a miss_reason (photo_not_joined, outside_tolerance, blurred, wrong_region). The targets_report is the feedback for planning: a consistent 0.3 m stand-off error tells the planner that its mount or localisation has a bias.
  9. Notify. gap-diff-ready on the event stream and the resource update. The planner reads get_gap_diff, updates its plan, and repeats until complete_for[purpose] is true or the operator dismisses what is left.

docs.title: 6. Changes needed
docs.text:
All proposals. Neither project writes into the other's repository; robotics-lab items go as messages, as the contract note records.

Recce.

  • Gap computation as a stage that writes gaps.json, with the RC-P3 quality state as its input. Thresholds are data in the ruleset.
  • A placement result in the reconstruction's frame (fit of the priors to the reconstruction, residual, rejected priors) so frame.placement exists. This sits on RC-P9.
  • Gap lineage and status in the metadata store (open question 3 of the sketch).
  • The verbs of section 4 on the three faces, one implementation behind them.
  • The manifest reader accepts site, frame, targets, and writes them back into gaps.json.
  • Fixtures: the RC-P9 Blender room with exact poses (expected: planar viewpoints usable), the kicker (expected: nothing usable, no_scale present), and one capture set with deliberately wrong priors (expected: no_scale critical for robots).
  • Image scope for landmark photos; gap lists never embed pixels. Home scans hold faces and documents, and the lists reveal room layout, so the retention rules of the sketch's §8 apply to gap lists too.

Robotics-lab (amendments to RFC-0025 §5.1, proposed).

  • "What we want back" gains gaps.json, with the frame rules of section 3.3.
  • The manifest gains site {id, frame_id}, frame_id for the pose frame (a run's map plus its start identity), and targets.
  • A goal kind for capture, in RFC-0014 §3.4.1's style: capture_view {pose or planar, tolerance, burst {photos, baseline_deg}, gap_ids}, done when the burst is recorded, result naming the capture set. Without it, a planner can send the robot to the stand pose but nothing triggers the burst (RFC-0025 §5.1 leaves "who triggers a capture" open).
  • The robot file's capabilities gain a camera entry (mount, height, pitch range, field of view) so an actor profile is derived, not typed.
  • Site export carries the dock pose and the frame identity, so a planner proves a frame match.
  • A named place for a recon MCP server in the agent's configuration, beside mission-control, with its own token and client name.

docs.title: 7. Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Push (Recce calls Mission Control or a webhook) against pull (consumer reads). Pull wins. The seam is files and a command line, and neither project writes into the other (RFC-0025 §5); Recce does not know a consumer's address; a consumer that is offline loses nothing. A push adds failure handling for the consumer that Recce has no reason to own. A CLI --on-ready COMMAND hook is the one push offered, for local scripts.
  • A ROS-style action (CaptureViews.action: goal, feedback, result). Rejected as the primary shape. A capture-and-reconstruct session spans hours and days and many processes, so a goal-feedback-result pairing between two live nodes does not model it; a document persists, diffs, replays in a test, and is read by an agent or a human. robotics-lab is ROS-aligned in names, with no ROS foundation yet (ADR-0001) and a ROS 2 bridge only in MVP 2, so an action needs the bridge first. A thin adapter that publishes planar as geometry_msgs/PoseStamped can follow the bridge (inferred). An action does fit one case, live progress while the robot shoots a burst; that case is out of scope here.
  • Gaps inside provenance.json. Rejected. Provenance records how a result was made and is fixed by its hashes; gap status changes with every claim and re-run, and the gap ids must outlive any one reconstruction. The two documents point at each other by hash.
  • One document per purpose. Rejected for the list; accepted for the brief. The list stays purpose-neutral in evidence and carries all four rankings. gap_brief renders a per-purpose, per-actor view on request.
  • Recce emits Mission Control goals. Rejected. It couples Recce to goal kinds, frames and guardrails it does not own, and a goal refused by a navigator would need a feedback path anyway. Recce emits poses and acceptance regions; the planner owns goals.
  • Route planning inside Recce. Rejected; idea 21 says "not route planning". Recce has no map.

docs.title: 8. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Gap matching across re-runs. Region overlap works while the frame is stable; after a re-solve in which the frame moves, matching can split or merge gaps. The rule needs evidence from RC-P1 runs of the same set with added photos.
  2. Gap thresholds and severity formulas (the 15 degrees and 3 photos are placeholders). RC-P3 sets them against ground truth; the ruleset field exists so changing them is visible.
  3. Actor profile format: Recce's own, or robotics-lab's robot file (VDA factsheet names, RFC-0014 §3.3.1) extended? One format would avoid a translation layer.
  4. MCP transport. Answered by robotics-lab (d): Recce's HTTP API on the tailnet with tokens, and a stdio MCP server on the agent's machine as its client.
  5. Whether the claim lease should be shorter for a robot than for a human, and whether Recce ever stops offering a gap a robot repeatedly missed (attempts is recorded; the policy is not).
  6. Frame identity: who mints frame_id for a run's map, and how a planner proves two ids describe the same frame after a relocalisation (RFC-0025 §3.6 "map <- world epochs" is not verified in code).
  7. Gaps on geometry that exists only in products (holes need a mesh). The schema is open-ended in kind; whether holes are listed by region or by mesh face ids is undecided.
  8. Which purposes exist beyond the four, and who owns their definitions: Recce, or the consumer passing weights to gap_brief.

docs.title: 9. Not covered
docs.text:
• Nothing is built or measured. The example numbers are invented; the field set is a design, not a result of running the engine. No gap has been computed by Recce yet.
  • The gap kinds after the first four: holes, blur and exposure, missing colour reference underwater, disconnected components. Their evidence fields, their close criteria and their viewpoints are not designed.
  • Underwater and aerial frames (GPS, ENU, refractive geometry) and any actor but phone and ground robot. The actor list names drone and arm without a design for them.
  • Live feedback while the robot shoots (a running "ghost camera" on the robot), and any on-device Recce.
  • The robotics-lab side beyond reading: I read the Mission Control contract, the MCP server and RFCs, not the planner module (planner.py), the navigator code, flotilla's approvals or the Gazebo and Nav2 bridge. Mission Control's /plan takes words and returns goals; how an LLM planner would consume a gap list is not designed, and no prompt is proposed here.
  • The yaw zero direction and quaternion order in robotics-lab are not stated in the documents I read (inferred in section 2); a code check of geometry.py and wire.py is still to be made.
  • Flotilla: how its policy and approvals (RFC-0005, RFC-0014 §3.4.7) gate a capture goal that a gap produced. The simulator-first rule is cited; the approval path is not.
  • Authorisation detail: token scopes are named, not specified; revocation and rotation follow robotics-lab's auth.py only by analogy (inferred).
  • Privacy beyond the sentence in section 6: retention of gap lists, redaction in shot-card images, and whether a landmark thumbnail may leave the tailnet.
  • Throughput and size: how large a gap list grows on a thousand-image set (a gap per region on a large site) and whether list_gaps needs paging; the limit of gaps in gap_brief is a parameter without a default.
  • The human shot card and the top-down map (idea 21, M2): this note does not change them; it shares their text field.
  • Validation of the design with a consumer: no robotics-lab maintainer has read it. It goes to that project as a message when the owner approves.

docs.title: GPU rental spec for RC-P7 (2026-11-24)
docs.text:
Decision input for the owner. RC-P7 (brief, "RC-P7 — Distribution on a large set") needs one rented GPU beside the GB10 and the X3. This note states what that machine must be, compares providers on prices read from their own pages today, recommends two options with a cost cap, and lists the launch and teardown steps. Nothing is rented and no account exists yet.

Tags: [V] the figure was read on the provider's own page or price API on 2026-11-24 (the URL is inline). [unverified] the figure comes from a search snippet, a third-party page, memory or an estimate, or the provider's page did not load. Estimates are marked as such.

docs.title: 1. What P7 needs from the rented machine
The job
docs.text:
RC-P7's criterion is dense depth per view split across the GB10, the X3 and one rented GPU, plus registration cut into clusters solved on different machines. The rented machine takes one slice of each.

  • Input: COLMAP's Graham Hall, 1,273 images, six archive parts totalling 11.78 GB [V] (graham-hall.zip 1.29 GB plus .z01 to .z05 at 2.10 GB each; sizes from the HTTP headers of the release assets listed on https://demuc.de/colmap/datasets/). The page gives no pixel size.
  • Dense slice: about one third of the views, roughly 425, through pycolmap.patch_match_stereo (CUDA), photometric then geometric pass. The slice is the unit the split assigns; the share per machine is set by the coordinator, so the rented GPU may get more or less.
  • Registration cluster (optional on this node): one overlapping cluster of roughly 400 images: GPU SIFT extraction, matching, then COLMAP incremental or GLOMAP mapping. This stage runs mostly on the CPU and fits the same node.
  • Not needed: gsplat. RC-P7 measures depth and registration, so the gsplat figure below only sizes the node if the owner later adds a splat to the same rental.

docs.title: GPU class and VRAM
docs.text:
Stage Measured on the GB10 in RC-P2 Consequence patch_match_stereo, 2000 px up to 1,483 MiB of GPU memory, 86.6% average GPU utilisation 8 GB would run it at 2000 px gsplat, 7,000 steps, 2000 px 4.95 GB peak torch memory, 6.6 GB process memory 12 GB is enough Full resolution (6048 x 4032 class) not measured unknown; PatchMatch memory grows with image area

Requirement: an NVIDIA GPU with at least 16 GB of VRAM and a CUDA 12 or CUDA 13 driver. 24 GB (RTX 4090, L4, A10, A5000) leaves room for a full-resolution run; 48 GB (L40S, A6000) removes the question. No Blackwell requirement: x86_64 and Ada or Ampere cards are enough, and the PyPI/conda wheels cover them.

Speed is the unknown. The GB10 took 30.8 s per view (1,168.7 s for 38 views at 2000 px, RC-P2). No rented card has been timed. Estimate: a 4090 or L40S runs 1x to 3x the GB10's rate, so 10 to 31 s per view; 425 views take 1.2 to 3.7 h. The first 20 views on the rented node replace this estimate with a measurement.

docs.title: CPU, RAM, disk
docs.text:
Item Requirement Basis vCPU 8 or more feature extraction, fusion and mapping run on the CPU RAM 32 GB minimum, 64 GB preferred the dense run raised host memory by 10 GB on the GB10, gsplat by 13 GB (RC-P2); mapping a 400-image cluster needs more Disk 200 GB archives 11.8 GB, extracted images about the same, dense workspace estimate below

Dense workspace: RC-P2's 38-view workspace is 3.1 GB at 2000 px, 82 MB per view (undistorted image, photometric and geometric depth, normals, consistency graph). Estimate for 425 views: 35 GB; for all 1,273: 104 GB. Keep the 200 GB disk so a larger share fits without a restart.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
The node pulls the images straight from the GitHub release, so the home uplink carries almost nothing.

Transfer Direction Size (estimate) Time Graham Hall archives GitHub to node 11.8 GB [V] minutes on a datacenter link Slice list, camera database, sparse model, scripts X3 to node under 1 GB seconds Geometric depth maps for 425 views (float32, 2000 x 1295 is 10.4 MB each, uncompressed) node to X3 about 4.4 GB; about 13 GB for all 1,273 50 Mbit/s: 12 min (4.4 GB) or 35 min (13 GB); 500 Mbit/s: 1 to 3.5 min Registration cluster model node to X3 under 1 GB seconds

The X3's real uplink and downlink are not measured; the times above are arithmetic on the stated link speeds. If the dense step returns normals and photometric maps as well, the download is about 3x larger. Return only the geometric depth maps and the fused slice.

docs.title: OS and image
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 on x86_64, NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12 or 13.
  • Either a VM with root (Docker allowed), or a container pod. A VM runs tailscaled with a TUN device. A container pod usually has no TUN device and needs tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking, which makes the node reachable by SSH from the tailnet but not a route for other traffic [unverified].
  • Software: pycolmap with CUDA (RC-P1 and RC-P2 used conda-forge pycolmap=4.2.1, has_cuda True, on aarch64). Whether the x86_64 conda-forge build of the same version has a CUDA variant, and whether the colmap/colmap Docker image matches that version, are [unverified]; the first launch step checks pycolmap.has_cuda.

docs.title: Hours
docs.text: Phase Estimate Boot, Tailscale, environment, dataset download and extraction 0.5 to 1 h Dense depth, 425 views 1.2 to 3.7 h (section above) Registration cluster (SIFT, exhaustive match, mapping, about 400 images) 0.2 to 0.5 h; RC-P1 matched 38 images in 5 to 10 s and matching scales with pairs, so 400 images is about 100x; mapping scales worse Transfer back and checks 0.2 to 0.5 h Total 2 to 5 h; plan 5 h

docs.title: Access pattern
docs.text: SSH from the X3. Preferred: the node joins the owner's tailnet with an ephemeral, tagged auth key and the X3 reaches it by its tailnet name; no public SSH port is exposed. Fallback: plain SSH to the provider's public IP with a key, restricted to the X3's address where the provider has a firewall. The coordinator on the X3 pushes work over SSH and pulls results with rsync.

docs.title: 3. Recommendation
docs.text:
Cheapest sensible: RunPod, RTX 4090 24 GB, Community Cloud, $0.34 per hour [V]. Per-second billing, no egress fee, any container image, 24 GB covers a full-resolution trial. Fall back to Secure Cloud at $0.89 per hour if the Community pod is slow to start or reclaimed. Cost for a 5-hour run:

Item Cost Compute, 5 h at $0.34 $1.70 (Secure: $4.45) Disk, 200 GB container disk at $0.10/GB/month, about 6 h about $0.17 Egress and ingress $0 Total about $2 (Secure: about $5)

Cap: load $10 of prepaid credit and no more; the pod stops itself at a zero balance [V]. Teardown when the run ends regardless of the balance.

More reliable: Scaleway L40S-1-48G, EUR 1.40 per hour [unverified], Paris or Warsaw. A full VM with root (TUN device, Docker, plain Tailscale), 48 GB of VRAM, an EU operator and EU data location. The price rests on a search snippet because the pricing page refused the fetch tool; the owner confirms it in the console before launch. If Scaleway's GPU quota or stock blocks the launch, AWS g6e.xlarge in eu-north-1 (L40S, $1.974 per hour [V]) is the fallback with a verified price.

Item Cost Compute, 5 h at EUR 1.40 EUR 7.00 Block storage, 200 GB for 6 h under EUR 1 [unverified] Egress not read [unverified]; the depth maps are about 4 to 13 GB Total about EUR 8

Cap: EUR 20, set as a billing alert and enforced by deleting the instance at the 8-hour mark.

The cheap option gives the first measurement. The reliable one covers the case where Community hardware misbehaves (disk speed, reclaim) and distorts the wall-clock number P7 records.

docs.title: 4. Launch checklist
docs.text:
Owner actions are marked (owner). No account, key or resource is created by the agent.

  1. Account (owner). Create the provider account (RunPod first). Use the email of record and turn on two-factor authentication.
  2. Payment (owner). RunPod: add prepaid credit of $10. Scaleway: add a card and set a billing alert at EUR 20. Do not enable auto top-up.
  3. SSH key (owner). Add the public key of the X3's ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub in the provider console. The private key stays on the X3.
  4. Tailscale auth key (owner). In the Tailscale admin console create an auth key that is ephemeral, reusable off, pre-approved, tagged (for example tag:rental), with an expiry of 24 h. The owner creates it and pastes it into the node shell; the agent never receives it, and it is never committed. Add an ACL entry that lets the X3 reach tag:rental and nothing in the other direction.
  5. Image. RunPod: template runpod/pytorch with a CUDA 12.x tag (check the tag in the console), container disk 200 GB, GPU RTX 4090 Community. Scaleway: Ubuntu 24.04 GPU image with the NVIDIA driver, a 200 GB volume. Confirm with nvidia-smi that the driver reports CUDA 12 or 13.
  6. Join the tailnet (on the node). 
    curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
sudo tailscale up --auth-key="$TS_AUTHKEY" --hostname=recce-p7-rental --advertise-tags=tag:rental --ssh=false
    In a container pod with no TUN device: tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking --socket=/tmp/tailscaled.sock & then tailscale --socket=/tmp/tailscaled.sock up ... with the same flags. Check from the X3: tailscale ping recce-p7-rental and ssh root@recce-p7-rental nvidia-smi.
  7. Environment (on the node). Install micromamba and create the P1 environment: micromamba create -p ~/p7env -c conda-forge python=3.12 pycolmap=4.2.1 numpy. Run ~/p7env/bin/python -c "import pycolmap; print(pycolmap.has_cuda)". If it prints False, stop and record it; do not build COLMAP by hand without asking (the node costs money while idle).
  8. Data. On the node, pull the archives directly: 
    mkdir -p ~/p7/graham && cd ~/p7/graham
for f in graham-hall.zip graham-hall.z0{1..5}; do
  curl -fLO https://github.com/colmap/colmap/releases/download/3.11.1/$f; done
zip -FF graham-hall.zip --out graham-hall-combined.zip && unzip -q graham-hall-combined.zip
    From the X3, send the slice list, scripts and sparse model: rsync -avz --partial ~/.cache/recce/runs/p7/handoff/ root@recce-p7-rental:~/p7/handoff/.
  9. Run. Start the dense slice detached (long-job skill) and sample the GPU every 5 s as in RC-P2 (sample_gpu.sh). Time the first 20 views and compare with the 10 to 31 s per view estimate; if the rate is worse than the GB10's 30.8 s, stop and report before spending more hours.
  10. Pull results. rsync -avz --partial --info=progress2 root@recce-p7-rental:~/p7/out/ ~/.cache/recce/runs/p7/rental/. Record the byte count and the elapsed time.
  11. Teardown. Copy the results and the logs first, then delete the instance. RunPod: terminate the pod (a stopped pod with a volume still bills for the disk; stopped volume disk costs $0.20/GB/month [V]) and delete any network volume. Scaleway: delete the instance and its volumes and its flexible IP. The ephemeral Tailscale node disappears from the admin console after it goes offline; remove it by hand if it stays listed and revoke the auth key.
  12. Verify nothing keeps billing. Provider console: instances list empty, volumes list empty, IP list empty; the balance on RunPod (or the cost view on Scaleway) checked again after one hour and shows no movement. Tailscale admin: no tag:rental machine, auth key revoked.

docs.title: What P7 records
docs.text: Measure Where it comes from Wall-clock per phase (boot, setup, download, dense depth, registration, return) timestamps in the run log Seconds per view on the rented GPU, against the GB10's 30.8 s and the X3's figure first 20 views and the whole slice Transfer time and bytes, each direction, with the measured X3 link speed rsync summary Billed cost: compute, storage, egress, from the provider's invoice or balance, not the estimate console Idle time between rental start and the first dense view log timestamps GPU name, driver, CUDA, pycolmap build, has_cuda nvidia-smi, pip/conda list The result against the fastest single machine, and the break-even set size if splitting does not pay (the brief's closing sentence of RC-P7) RC-P7 results table

docs.title: 5. Not covered
docs.text:
• Real speed of any rented card. No GPU in this note was timed on PatchMatch. The 10 to 31 s per view range is an assumption of 1x to 3x the GB10; it can be wrong in both directions.
  • Full-resolution memory. RC-P2 measured 2000 px only. Graham Hall's pixel size is not on the dataset page, so the full-resolution VRAM and time are unknown.
  • x86_64 CUDA pycolmap. Not checked that a CUDA build of pycolmap 4.2.1 exists for x86_64 on conda-forge, or that the colmap/colmap image matches it.
  • Prices not read on a provider page: Vast.ai per-GPU prices (listing empty for the 4090 at fetch time), Scaleway (page returned 403; snippet only), OVHcloud per-GPU prices, Verda L40S and A100 prices (a snippet conflicts with the page), Genesis Cloud (TLS failure), and all of DigitalOcean's, Google Cloud's and Azure's egress and storage prices. Google Cloud's region per price column was not extracted.
  • Availability and stock. Whether an RTX 4090 Community pod, a Scaleway L40S, a Lambda GPU in europe-central-1 or a Hetzner server is free today was not checked; stock changes by the minute.
  • Quotas and sign-up friction. GPU quota requests, identity checks and approval waits at Google Cloud, AWS, Azure, Scaleway and OVHcloud were not tested; no account was created.
  • Tailscale inside RunPod pods. The userspace-networking route is the documented Tailscale mode for containers without TUN but was not run on RunPod.
  • Spot and interruptible reliability. Reclaim rates were not measured; the plan avoids spot for the timed run.
  • The X3's internet uplink and downlink. Not measured; every transfer time is arithmetic on a stated speed.
  • The X3 HIP path (RC-P2) and the GB10 schedule. The split's other two machines are outside this note; the rented GPU's share depends on them.
  • Tax. Prices exclude VAT unless the page said otherwise; the Lambda page states exclusion [V], the others were not checked.

docs.title: Hardware and parallelism
docs.text: Input to the brief. From the operator on 2026-11-23, plus what was read off the X3 itself.

docs.title: The machines
docs.text:
Machine CPU / GPU Memory GPU API Notes MacBook Pro M4 Pro Apple silicon 48 GB Metal Daily driver; the field machine. Apple Object Capture runs only here (and on iOS). DGX Spark (GB10) ARM64 + Blackwell, compute capability 12.1 128 GB unified CUDA 13 GPU shared with other workloads on a schedule, so its availability varies. ARM64 wheels missing for much of the stack. X3 (GMKtec EVO-X3) AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 32 threads, Radeon 8060S (RDNA 3.5) 128 GB ROCm/HIP or Vulkan Linux. The likely coordinator. ~~iMac Pro~~ Intel Xeon W, AMD Vega ≥ 64 GB Metal only, no CUDA Out of the design (2026-11-24). Most of the stack ships no macOS x86_64 wheels; its cost exceeds its contribution.

Four GPU platforms: CUDA, Metal, HIP/Vulkan and an older Metal-on-Intel. Existing tools mostly assume one NVIDIA box.

docs.title: Measured in Step 0 (2026-11-24)
docs.text:
• pycolmap packaging. PyPI's pycolmap 4.2.1 has wheels for x86_64 Linux, Apple silicon and Windows, all CPU only: no CUDA, no Metal, no Linux ARM. On the GB10, conda-forge's CUDA build (through micromamba, user-level) runs SIFT extraction and matching on the GPU, about three times faster than the CPU on the X3 or the M4 Pro (RC-P1).
  • The GB10's schedule. In gpu-mode prod the production LLMs leave about 15 GB of the 121 GB free. Recce GPU work runs in a free window (by day under the owner's standing go; the homelab session switches back to prod and verifies). CUDA dense depth plus a gsplat run peaked at 50 GB used (RC-P2).
  • Memory. Registering a 38-image ETH3D scene peaks at 28 GB resident (M4 Pro).
  • The X3's GPU. No ROCm on the host. COLMAP main (HIP backend since 2026-10) built in a ROCm 7.2.4 container runs dense depth on gfx1151 at about 2.7 times the GB10's time; one intermittent abort.
  • Mapping speed. On the busy X3 COLMAP's incremental mapper took 57 s on kicker, the M4 Pro 17 s, the GB10 22 s; GLOMAP 3–4 times faster on every machine.

Summary of all findings: Step 0 status and findings.

docs.title: The operator's goal, in their words (paraphrased)
docs.text: Large photo sets in large formats need parallelism, and existing projects don't use the hardware well. Use everything available: a GPU where there is one, other machines through workers that are deployed to them, and possibly more machines later. Something easy works on the laptop alone. In the field, the laptop uploads photos; the main service may run on the X3 and hand work to the GB10 and others. Full flexibility; explore every form of parallelism.

docs.title: Forms of parallelism to explore
docs.text:
1. Per-item fan-out — feature extraction per image, matching per pair, depth per view. Embarrassingly parallel; most of the hours.
  2. Spatial partitioning — split a large scene into overlapping clusters, reconstruct each on a different machine, merge. COLMAP's hierarchical mapper does this on one box.
  3. Streaming pipeline — work starts while photos are still arriving; the laptop builds a quick preview, bigger machines take later stages.
  4. Comparative runs — classical and learned pipelines side by side on different machines, the difference itself a quality signal.
  5. Capability placement — workers advertise CUDA / Metal / HIP / CPU, memory and availability (including whether a shared GPU is free); the coordinator places each stage. Workers join and leave.

docs.title: Capture devices, in the order the operator plans to test
docs.text:
1. iPhone 15 Pro (ProRAW, LiDAR, ARKit poses)
  2. GoPro
  3. Nikon D850 and Sony Alpha 1 (RAW)
  4. DJI Mini 4 Pro drone
  5. Robots, with depth cameras and possibly motorised sliders still to choose

Underwater photography is a first-class interest of the operator, not an edge case.

docs.title: Public datasets for Recce Step 0: drone and smartphone captures
docs.text:
Date of search: 2026-11-26, by a research subagent; the EuroSDR RPAS record (licence CC BY 4.0, 43.1 GB, Phase 2 9.9 GB) was re-checked against Zenodo's API afterwards. Method: web search plus fetch of dataset pages, repositories, Zenodo records and papers. Nothing was downloaded. Where a fact comes from a search snippet and not from a page I fetched, or a page was silent, the item appears under "Could not verify".

Already known and not re-checked here: OpenDroneMap sample sets (no ground truth), ARKitScenes (in use), ETH3D, Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples.

Brief mention of known sets: OpenDroneMap samples (no ground truth), ETH3D (DSLR, TLS ground truth), Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples (ground-level), all outside the new work here.

docs.title: Best three for Group A
docs.text:
1. EuroSDR RPAS benchmark. CC BY 4.0, surveyed checkpoints, GCPs, a TLS cloud and a road profile, and the same site flown with no RTK and with RTK. It is the only candidate where drone GPS quality is the experiment variable, so it answers the pose-prior question the way RC-P8 did for ETH3D and ARKitScenes. The 9.9 GB Phase 2 file keeps the first fetch small; the P1 flight reaches about 1,000 images.
  2. GauU-Scene V2. CC BY 4.0 (stated in the paper), six scenes of 424 to 1,215 images with drone-log georeferencing and a LiDAR reference. Use it for the 1,000+ image and coverage-report tests. Its LiDAR alignment is fitted, so do not use it as an absolute-scale oracle.
  3. UseGeo. LiDAR reference, ground-truth depth and 829 images at 7952 x 5304, small enough to run whole. Non-commercial and share-alike, so it suits internal prototypes and published results only, not shipped fixtures. Mill 19 is the fallback for a scale-only distribution test with no ground truth.
